Every row increases, as it must, and at order 10 the divergence is already within 7% of the worst case. The larger of the die’s two ratios has probability \(\frac12\) under \(P\), so the power mean reaches the maximum quickly.
The Rényi divergence also bounds how often the evidence is large. Suppose the data come from \(Q\), and you ask how often an observation gives at least some number \(c\) of nats of evidence for \(P\). The Chernoff method of Concentration inequalities answers this with Markov’s inequality. That inequality says that a quantity that cannot be negative exceeds a level with probability at most its average divided by the level. Apply it to \(r^\alpha\), which reaches \(e^{\alpha c}\) exactly when the evidence reaches \(c\). The order must be positive here, because only then does \(r^\alpha\) rise with the evidence. By the definition, the average of \(r^\alpha\) under \(Q\) is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha}\). Dividing it by \(e^{\alpha c}\) gives, for every order \(\alpha > 0\), \[Q[L \ge c] \le \exp\big(-\alpha c + (\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)\big). \tag{3.6}\]
At order 1 the bound is \(e^{-c}\), Markov’s inequality applied to \(r\) itself, and it holds for every pair of distributions. The KL divergence, the order-1 member, drops out of the bound entirely, because an average says nothing about how often a quantity is far from it. Larger orders use more about the pair and can do much better.

title: 3  Divergences
section: 3.4 Two normal distributions with equal variance
text:
3.4 Two normal distributions with equal variance
The most common pair in practice is a distribution and a shifted copy of it. It describes the same noise around two different centres, a feature before and after a drift, or two classes with the same spread. For two normal distributions with equal variance, every divergence has a closed form.
Let \(P\) be a normal distribution centred at 0, and write \(\sigma\) for its standard deviation. Let \(Q\) be the same curve shifted to the right by a distance \(s\). What matters is how far apart the centres are compared with the width of the curves. So write \(\mu = s/\sigma\) for the shift measured in standard deviations. Probability distributions showed that the evidence for this pair is a straight line in \(x\): \[L(x) = \frac{s^2 - 2sx}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{3.7}\] The divergences follow from this line: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \frac{\mu^2}2, \qquad D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{\alpha\mu^2}2, \qquad D_\infty(P\|Q) = \infty. \tag{3.8}\]
Each formula has a one-line reason. The KL divergence is the average of a straight line, which is the line’s value at the average point 0. The Rényi divergence grows linearly in the order because the evidence is itself normal under \(P\), and averages of exponentials of a normal quantity have a simple closed form. The max-divergence is infinite because a line with a non-zero slope is unbounded.
Three consequences matter in practice. First, only the signal-to-noise ratio \(\mu\) matters, so doubling the noise has the same effect as halving the shift. Second, the dependence on the shift is quadratic, so a small shift costs very little. A shift of 0.1 standard deviations gives a KL divergence of only 0.005, which is why a small drift needs many samples to see. Third, the divergences add over independent coordinates. A shift by a vector in many dimensions, with the same standard deviation in each, gives \(\alpha\) times its squared length over \(2\sigma^2\). Only the length of the shift matters, not its direction.
The average case is finite, while the worst case is infinite. Large likelihood ratios exist, but they are rare, and the tail bound Equation 3.6 says how rare. Take \(\mu = 1\). Then the KL divergence is 0.5 and \(D_2\) is 1. At order 10 the Rényi divergence reaches 5.
Now ask how often a draw from \(Q\) gives at least 2 nats of evidence for \(P\). Such a draw is about 7.4 times more likely under \(P\), although it came from \(Q\). Write \(\Phi\) for the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution. Because the evidence is a straight line, the event is a simple tail of \(Q\). The full edition works out its probability as \(\Phi(-\mu/2 - c/\mu)\), where \(c\) is the threshold in nats, and here that is \(\Phi(-2.5) = 0.0062\).
How close does the tail bound come? At order 1 it is Markov’s bound \(e^{-2} = 0.1353\), valid for any pair. For the normal pair you can choose the order. Because \(D_\alpha\) grows linearly in the order, the exponent of the bound is a parabola in it, and its lowest point is at order 2.5. There the bound is \(e^{-3.125} = 0.0439\). So the Rényi bound is 7 times the exact value, against 22 times for Markov’s. The remaining gap is the usual price of the Chernoff method. Markov’s inequality is exact only for a quantity that takes just two values, and the evidence here is spread out.

title: 3  Divergences
section: 3.5 Two Laplace distributions with shifted location
text:
3.5 Two Laplace distributions with shifted location
The Laplace distribution is the other standard noise model. Its density falls off like \(e^{-|x - m|/b}\) on both sides of its centre \(m\), where the scale \(b\) sets its width. So it has a sharp peak, and its tails fall off exponentially, more slowly than the normal’s. Probability distributions showed that its evidence against a shifted copy is bounded, unlike the normal’s. This section shows what that difference does to the divergences.
Let \(P\) be the Laplace distribution centred at 0 with scale \(b\). Let \(Q\) be the same distribution shifted to the right by a distance \(s\). Write \(t = s/b\) for the shift measured in units of the scale. The max-divergence is just the shift, and the KL divergence is slightly less: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = t + e^{-t} - 1, \qquad D_\infty(P\|Q) = t. \tag{3.9}\] With scale 1, the evidence is \(L(x) = |x - t| - |x|\), the difference of the two exponents. Two numbers that are \(t\) apart cannot have absolute values that differ by more than \(t\). So the evidence never exceeds \(t\) in either direction. For every \(x \le 0\), the evidence equals \(t\) exactly. That region has probability \(\frac12\) under \(P\), so the worst case is not rare at all. Every Rényi divergence of this pair also has a closed form, given with the cheat sheet in Equation 3.20.
Figure 3.3 shows where each order looks, which is at \(P\) reweighted toward large likelihood ratios, more strongly as the order grows. For the normal pair the reweighting slides into the tail forever, so the Rényi divergence grows without bound. For the Laplace pair it piles up on \(x \le 0\), where the evidence is already at its maximum, and stops.






Figure 3.3: Where the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) looks: the normalized weights \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) for \(\alpha = 1, 2, 4, 8\). Left: \(\mathcal N(0, 2)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, 2)\); the weight is \(\mathcal N(1 - \alpha, 2)\) and runs off into the left tail. Right: \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, 1)\); the weight collects on \(x \le 0\) (shaded), where the log-likelihood ratio is already at its maximum, and stops.



To compare the two noise models fairly, give them the same variance. The Laplace distribution with scale \(b\) has variance \(2b^2\). A normal pair with that variance and the same shift has \(\mu = t/\sqrt2\), so its Rényi divergence is \(\alpha t^2/4\).
For small shifts, the Laplace pair is further apart. Its KL divergence is then close to \(t^2/2\), twice the normal pair’s \(t^2/4\). The Laplace density’s sharp peak makes a small shift easier to detect, because the peak moves visibly. For large orders the comparison reverses. The normal pair’s Rényi divergence grows linearly in the order forever. The Laplace pair’s rises and levels off at \(t\), because its likelihood ratio can never exceed \(e^t\). At \(t = 1\), the full edition’s script finds that the curves cross at order 2.98. Above that order, the normal pair is the more distinguishable one (Table 3.4, Figure 3.4). So a claim that one pair is “more different” than another must name the divergence.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.6 Total variation
The KL and Rényi divergences are convenient to compute, but they do not directly answer practical questions such as how often a test is right. The total variation (TV) does. Draw \(p\) and \(q\) on the same axes. Where the curves overlap, an observation cannot tell you which distribution produced it. Where they don’t, it can. The total variation is the part that does not overlap, the mass of \(P\) that sits above \(Q\).
The total variation has several equal forms. Each says the same thing from a different side: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \max_A|P(A) - Q(A)| = \sum_x\big(p(x) - q(x)\big)_+ = \frac12\sum_x|p(x) - q(x)|. \tag{3.10}\] Here \((y)_+\) means \(\max(y, 0)\), the positive part of a number \(y\). The first form is the largest gap between the probabilities of one event. The second is the mass where \(p\) sits above \(q\). The third is half the total absolute difference between the two probability tables. The overlap of the two curves, \(\sum_x\min(p(x), q(x))\), is one minus the total variation.
The forms agree because the largest gap \(P(A) - Q(A)\) comes from the event that collects every outcome where \(p > q\), and nothing else. The positive and negative differences \(p - q\) have equal total mass, since both distributions sum to 1, and that gives the half-sum form.
On the die, only the six has \(p > q\). Its excess is \(0.5 - \frac16 = \frac13\), so the total variation is \(\frac13\). Unlike the KL divergence, the total variation is symmetric, and it always lies between 0 and 1.
The total variation sets the limit for a single observation. Suppose \(P\) or \(Q\) is picked with probability \(\frac12\) each, and you see one draw. A test that says “\(P\)” on an event \(A\) is right in two cases. The draw came from \(P\) and landed in \(A\), or it came from \(Q\) and landed outside. Averaging the two cases gives a probability of \(\frac12 + \frac12(P(A) - Q(A))\). The best test therefore uses the best event, and says “\(P\)” exactly when the observation is more likely under \(P\). Its probability of being right is \[\Pr[\text{correct}] = \frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}(P, Q). \tag{3.11}\]
Guessing blind is right half the time, and seeing the draw adds half the total variation. A randomized test does no better, because it only mixes events, and a mix cannot beat the best one. The equal chances of \(P\) and \(Q\) are a condition of this formula. With unequal chances, the best test changes, and the hockey-stick divergence of the next section takes over.
On the die, the best test says “loaded” exactly when it sees a six. It is right with probability \(\frac12 + \frac16 = \frac23\). No classifier, however clever, can beat \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}\) from a single draw with equal chances, because this test already reaches it.
The total variation also bounds how much any fixed procedure can change when the data distribution changes. Let \(g\) be any statistic whose values always lie in an interval of length \(\ell\). Then its average moves by at most \(\ell\) times the total variation when \(Q\) is replaced by \(P\). For values between 0 and 1, the reason is that the change adds up \(g(x)\) times \(p(x) - q(x)\) over all outcomes. That sum is largest when \(g\) is 1 where \(p > q\) and 0 elsewhere, and then it equals the total variation.
For example, suppose the test distribution moves from \(Q\) to \(P\) with total variation at most 0.01. Then the accuracy of any fixed classifier moves by at most 0.01. Its accuracy is the average of a statistic that is 1 for a correct prediction and 0 for a wrong one. The classifier must stay fixed. A classifier retrained on the new data is a different statistic, and the bound says nothing about it.
The total variation does not add over samples. For \(n\) independent samples, it is capped at 1 and has no simple formula. That is why you usually compute a KL or Rényi divergence for \(n\) samples, where additivity makes it easy, and convert to total variation at the end (Section 3.10).
For the normal pair, the best event collects the outcomes more likely under \(P\). The two bell curves cross at the midpoint \(s/2\), so the best event is everything below it. Measured in standard deviations, the midpoint lies \(\mu/2\) above the centre of the first curve and the same distance below the centre of the second. This gives \[\mathrm{TV} = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2\Big) - \Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2\Big) = 2\Phi\Big(\frac\mu2\Big) - 1. \tag{3.12}\] At \(\mu = 1\) the total variation is 0.3829. The best test is then right with probability 0.6915 (Figure 3.5, left).






Figure 3.5: Left: two unit-variance Gaussians one standard deviation apart. The shaded area, where \(p\) exceeds \(q\), is the total variation, and the best test thresholds at the midpoint. Right: the best accuracy for telling \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) from \(\mathcal N(0.1, 1)\) as the number of samples grows, exactly, by simulation, and as bounded through Pinsker’s inequality.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.7 Hockey-stick divergence
The total variation measures the mass of \(p\) that sticks out above \(q\). Now scale \(q\) up by a factor \(\gamma\) of at least 1. Then measure the mass of \(p\) that still sticks out above \(\gamma q\) (Figure 3.6). Only outcomes where \(p\) is more than \(\gamma\) times \(q\) count. This is the hockey-stick divergence, written \(E_\gamma\). It measures how much of the difference between the two distributions comes from likelihood ratios above \(\gamma\): \[E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \max_A\big[P(A) - \gamma Q(A)\big] = \sum_x\big(p(x) - \gamma q(x)\big)_+ = \mathbb E_Q\big[(r - \gamma)_+\big]. \tag{3.13}\] The name comes from the shape of \((r - \gamma)_+\) as a function of \(r\), flat and then a straight line. As for the total variation, the best event collects every outcome where \(p\) beats \(\gamma q\).






Figure 3.6: The hockey-stick divergence as an area, for \(p = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(q = \mathcal N(1, 1)\). Raising \(\gamma\) lifts the curve \(\gamma q\), and \(E_\gamma\) is the shaded mass of \(p\) still above it: 0.3829 (the total variation) at \(\gamma = 1\), then 0.1906 and 0.0692. It shrinks but never reaches zero, because \(r\) is unbounded in the left tail.



The condition \(\gamma \ge 1\) is what makes this a divergence. With \(\gamma\) below 1, take the event that contains every outcome. It gives \(1 - \gamma\), so the quantity would be positive even for two equal distributions.
Three properties follow from the picture. With no scaling, the hockey-stick divergence is the total variation, so \(E_1 = \mathrm{TV}\). As \(\gamma\) grows, less of \(p\) sticks out, so \(E_\gamma\) never increases. It reaches zero exactly when \(\gamma q\) covers \(p\) everywhere. That happens once \(\gamma\) reaches the largest likelihood ratio, \(e^{D_\infty}\).
A fourth property is the reason the divergence matters for testing. Write \(\pi\) for the prior probability of \(P\), the chance that \(P\) produced the data before you look at them. Assume that this prior is at most one half, so that the prior odds against \(P\), written \(\gamma = (1 - \pi)/\pi\), are at least 1. The smallest possible chance of a wrong guess from one observation is then \(\pi(1 - E_\gamma(P\|Q))\). The reason is that a test that says “\(P\)” on an event \(A\) errs with probability \(\pi(1 - [P(A) - \gamma Q(A)])\). The best event makes the bracket equal to \(E_\gamma\). So always guessing \(Q\) is wrong with probability \(\pi\), and the observation removes a fraction \(E_\gamma\) of that error. With equal priors, \(\gamma\) is 1, and this is the total-variation test of the previous section.
For the normal pair, the full edition computes the hockey-stick divergence in closed form: \[E_\gamma = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac{\ln\gamma}\mu\Big) - \gamma\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac{\ln\gamma}\mu\Big). \tag{3.14}\] It is positive for every \(\gamma\), because the max-divergence is infinite and no finite \(\gamma\) covers \(p\). At \(\mu = 1\) it gives \(E_2 = 0.1906\). For the Laplace pair, the formula is \(1 - e^{-(t - \ln\gamma)/2}\) as long as \(\gamma\) is at most \(e^t\). Beyond that point it is zero. At \(\gamma = 1\) this gives the Laplace total variation, \(1 - e^{-t/2}\).
The curve of \(E_\gamma\) against \(\gamma\) shows how much of the difference comes from large likelihood ratios (Figure 3.7). For the die, only the six has a ratio above \(\gamma\), for \(\gamma\) between 1 and 3. So \(E_\gamma = 0.5 - \gamma/6\) falls in a straight line to zero at \(\gamma = 3\). The Laplace curve reaches zero at \(\ln\gamma = t\), while the normal curve never does. So the curve separates a ratio that is never large, as for the Laplace pair, from one that is large only rarely, as for the normal pair.






Figure 3.7: The hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma(P\|Q)\) against \(\ln\gamma\) for the loaded die, a Laplace pair and a normal pair with the same variance. The die and Laplace curves reach zero at their max-divergences; the normal curve stays positive.



Rejection sampling shows what the hockey-stick divergence costs in practice. It draws samples from a target \(p\) using draws from an easier proposal \(q\). You propose an outcome from \(q\) and keep it with probability \(\min(1, p/(\gamma q))\). This works exactly when the envelope \(\gamma q\) lies above \(p\) everywhere. If \(\gamma\) is too small, the part of \(p\) above the envelope is cut off. The mass of that part is exactly \(E_\gamma\).
Take the loaded die as the target and the fair die as the proposal. With \(\gamma = 3\), the largest ratio, the envelope covers \(p\), and the samples have exactly the loaded die’s distribution. With \(\gamma = 2\), the envelope gives a six only \(\frac13\), less than the loaded die gives it. The uncovered mass is \(E_2 = 0.5 - \frac13 = \frac16\). The kept rolls are in proportion to the smaller of \(p\) and the envelope, which is 0.1 for each other face and \(\frac13\) for the six. These add up to \(\frac56\). After dividing by that total, a six comes up 40% of the time instead of 50%. The total variation between the output and the target is \(0.5 - 0.4 = 0.1\), below \(E_2\). In general it is at most \(E_\gamma\), so the hockey-stick divergence bounds what a cheap envelope costs. The bound is loose because dividing by the total gives back part of the mass that was cut off.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.8 f-divergences
The KL divergence, the total variation and the hockey-stick divergence were defined separately. But each is an average under \(Q\) of some function of the likelihood ratio. Naming the function gives one family, the f-divergences, with one proof of their properties for all members.
Pick a function \(f\) of a positive number \(t\) that meets two conditions. It must be convex, which means its graph bends upward like a bowl. And it must be zero at \(t = 1\), so that a ratio of 1, no evidence either way, counts as no difference. The f-divergence averages \(f\) of the likelihood ratio under \(Q\): \[D_f(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_Q\big[f(r(X))\big] = \sum_xq(x)\,f\Big(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\Big). \tag{3.15}\] Table 3.5 lists the common choices of \(f\), called generators, with their values on the die.

Every f-divergence is at least 0, and the two conditions on \(f\) are what guarantee it. Under \(Q\), the likelihood ratio averages to exactly 1, provided \(Q\) gives positive probability to every outcome \(P\) can produce. Otherwise the average falls short of 1 by the mass of \(P\) that \(Q\) misses. For a convex function, the average of the function is at least the function of the average. So the f-divergence is at least \(f(1)\), which is 0. A generator that is not convex could give a negative value, and one that is not zero at 1 would not vanish for equal distributions.
The Rényi divergence is not an f-divergence. But it is an increasing function of the one with generator \(t^\alpha - 1\), or \(1 - t^\alpha\) for orders below one, so it inherits their properties.
Figure 3.8 shows how each generator weighs the likelihood ratio. The \(\chi^2\) divergence grows quadratically in the ratio, so outcomes with large ratios dominate it. On the die it is 0.80, the largest entry in Table 3.5. The total variation and the hockey-stick divergence grow linearly and ignore every ratio below a threshold. The reverse KL divergence blows up as the ratio goes to 0, so it punishes outcomes that \(P\) almost never produces.






Figure 3.8: The generator functions \(f\) of six f-divergences, as functions of the likelihood ratio \(t = p/q\). All are convex and vanish at \(t = 1\). The dotted lines mark the two likelihood ratios of the loaded die.



The hockey-stick curves determine every f-divergence. The reason is that any convex generator can be built from hockey-stick shapes, one bend at each threshold, weighted by how sharply the generator bends there. So if you know the hockey-stick curves in both directions for every \(\gamma\) of at least 1, you know every f-divergence and every Rényi divergence. Later parts use this to move between different ways of saying that two distributions are close.
The f-divergences can also be estimated from samples alone, without knowing either density. A variant of the generative adversarial network (GAN) uses this to train generative models. It is called the f-GAN (Nowozin, Cseke & Tomioka, 2016).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.9 The data processing inequality
You rarely look at raw data. You bin it, compute features, threshold a score, or pass it through a randomized algorithm. The data processing inequality (DPI) says that none of this can make two distributions easier to tell apart.
The reason is that processing averages likelihood ratios. When processing maps several inputs to the same output, the output’s likelihood ratio is an average of the inputs’ ratios, weighted by how likely each input is under \(Q\). Averaging pulls strong evidence toward weak evidence. Suppose you report only whether a die roll is even. A six, with ratio 3, is then reported together with a two and a four, with ratio 0.6 each. The fair die weighs the three rolls equally, so the even result gets the moderate ratio \((3 + 0.6 + 0.6)/3 = 1.4\). Every divergence is a convex summary of the ratios. For a convex summary, averaging first can only make it smaller, so no divergence can grow.
Processing may be random, so describe it by its output probabilities. A channel, written \(K\), maps each input \(x\) to a distribution over outputs \(y\). A deterministic function is the special case that puts all its probability on one output. Feeding draws from each distribution through the channel gives two output distributions, written \(PK\) and \(QK\). The inequality says that the outputs are never further apart than the inputs. For every f-divergence and every channel, \[D_f(PK\|QK) \le D_f(P\|Q). \tag{3.16}\] The same holds for every Rényi divergence, because each is an increasing function of an f-divergence. It holds for the max-divergence too, which is their limit.
The channel may use its own randomness, but one condition is essential. The channel must be the same whether the input came from \(P\) or from \(Q\). A channel that behaved differently in the two cases would carry information about which one it saw, and the output could then be easier to tell apart than the input.
Nothing is lost when the processing keeps the likelihood ratio, that is, when \(r(x)\) can be computed from the output. Such an output is called a sufficient statistic, and for it the inequality holds with equality. Table 3.6 shows the die reduced to its parity.

On the even rolls, the strong evidence of a six is diluted by the twos and fours. The KL divergence drops from 0.2939 for the full roll to 0.0823 for its parity. If you instead report only whether the roll is a six, nothing is lost. The likelihood ratio depends only on that bit, so the bit is sufficient, and the KL divergence stays at 0.2939.
The coarsest processing reports only whether some event \(A\) happened. That turns each distribution into a coin, whose probability of heads is the probability it gives to the event. Write \(a\) and \(b\) for the heads probabilities of two coins. The KL divergence between the coins is called the binary KL divergence: \[\mathrm{kl}(a, b) = a\ln\frac ab + (1 - a)\ln\frac{1-a}{1-b}. \tag{3.17}\] By the inequality, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) is at least \(\mathrm{kl}(P(A), Q(A))\) for every event \(A\). So if the KL divergence is small, no event can have very different probabilities under \(P\) and \(Q\). Hypothesis testing uses this form to bound the errors of any test.
In practice, there is no free lunch from processing. A feature extractor, a summary statistic or a quantizer can only lose information about which distribution produced the data. The DPI bounds the best test, not a particular classifier. A processing step can help a bad classifier, but it cannot beat the best test on the raw data.
Binning a normal observation shows how much each divergence loses. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be standard normal curves centred at 0 and at 1, with KL divergence 0.5. Suppose a sensor rounds each observation into bins of some width \(w\), with a bin edge at the midpoint \(\frac12\). Within each bin, the straight line of the evidence is replaced by a single level, so wider bins average away more evidence (Figure 3.9). Table 3.7 gives the KL divergence after binning.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.10 Pinsker’s inequality
The KL divergence is easy to compute and adds up over samples. The total variation is what you usually want to report, because it gives the accuracy of the best test and the largest change in any bounded statistic. Pinsker’s inequality turns the first into a bound on the second. It says that the total variation is at most the square root of half the KL divergence: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) \le \sqrt{\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}. \tag{3.18}\]
The square root comes from how the two divergences grow for nearby distributions. Write the likelihood ratio as one plus a small relative difference. The total variation is half the average size of that difference, so it grows linearly in it. The KL divergence is approximately half the average of its square, as a second-order expansion of the logarithm shows, so it grows quadratically. The average size of a quantity is at most the square root of its average square. Putting these together gives Pinsker’s inequality for nearby distributions, constant included. The full edition proves it for all distributions by reducing any pair to a pair of coins.
The bound passes 1 once the KL divergence exceeds 2, and the total variation is never above 1. So for large KL divergences, use the Bretagnolle–Huber inequality instead. It stays below 1 for every KL divergence: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) \le \sqrt{1 - e^{-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}}. \tag{3.19}\] Solving for where the two bounds cross shows that Bretagnolle–Huber is the better bound once the KL divergence is above 1.59 (Figure 3.11).






Figure 3.11: Total variation against KL for shifted Gaussian pairs, shifted Laplace pairs and the die, with the Pinsker and Bretagnolle–Huber bounds. Every pair lies below both bounds; Pinsker is close near KL \(= 0\) and vacuous beyond KL \(= 2\).



The constant in Pinsker’s inequality cannot be improved, because the bound is tight for two coins with heads probabilities just above and just below one half. Normal pairs are not that extreme. For them the bound is \(\mu/2\), while the exact total variation is close to \(0.40\mu\) for small shifts.
The main use is to find how many samples you need. The KL divergence of \(n\) independent samples is \(n\) times that of one sample. So Pinsker’s inequality bounds the total variation of \(n\) samples by \(\sqrt{n\,\mathrm{KL}_1/2}\), where \(\mathrm{KL}_1\) is the KL divergence of one sample. By Equation 3.11, the best accuracy is then at most \(\frac12 + \frac12\sqrt{n\,\mathrm{KL}_1/2}\). For that bound to get close to 1, the product \(n\,\mathrm{KL}_1\) must be of order 1. So any test needs on the order of \(1/\mathrm{KL}_1\) samples to get close to perfect accuracy.
Take the normal pair with a shift of 0.1 standard deviations. One sample has KL divergence 0.005 and total variation only 0.0399, so the shift is invisible in a single observation. Table 3.8 shows how a few hundred samples make it clear, and compares the bounds with the exact total variation.

There is no converse, since a small total variation says nothing about the KL divergence. Suppose \(Q\) is a copy of \(P\), except that it moves a probability of \(10^{-9}\) onto a new outcome. Then the total variation is only \(10^{-9}\). But \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)\) is infinite, because \(Q\) produces an outcome to which \(P\) gives probability zero.

The Rényi divergence of the Laplace pair, for orders other than \(\frac12\) and 1, is \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)t} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha t}\right). \tag{3.20}\] At order \(\frac12\) both coefficients divide by zero, and the bracket is replaced by its limit \((1 + \frac t2)e^{-t/2}\).
Rules of thumb

KL is the rate at which evidence accumulates. Telling two distributions apart takes about \(1/\mathrm{KL}\) independent samples.
Compute in KL or Rényi, where independent samples add, and convert to TV at the end with Pinsker or Bretagnolle–Huber.
The Rényi order is a dial from typical evidence (order near 1) to the worst case (order going to infinity).
A bounded likelihood ratio (Laplace) gives a finite max-divergence. An unbounded one (normal) gives \(D_\infty = \infty\), though every finite order stays finite.
Processing averages likelihood ratios together, so it can never increase a divergence, as long as the processing is the same for both distributions.
Maximum likelihood minimizes forward KL and covers all modes. Variational inference minimizes reverse KL and picks one.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.13 Further reading

van Erven & Harremoës, “Rényi Divergence and Kullback–Leibler Divergence” (IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2014): the Rényi family and its properties, including proofs for general measures.
Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2nd ed., 2006), ch. 2 and §11.6: KL, Jensen’s inequality and Pinsker’s inequality.
Polyanskiy & Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning (2025), ch. 7: f-divergences, their variational forms and data processing at reference depth.
Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), §10.1: forward against reverse KL in variational inference.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, except the sample-based estimation of f-divergences, which it cites, and the bound on rejection sampling, which is an exercise there.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.1 Why this matters
A spam filter reads an email and must say “ham”, meaning a legitimate email, or “spam”. A fraud detector sees a transaction and must say “normal” or “fraud”. A monitoring job reads a batch of sensor readings and must say whether the sensor has drifted. These are all the same problem. An observation came from one of two distributions, and you must decide which one. Hypothesis testing is the study of that decision.
Later parts of this book ask how well any test could tell two distributions apart, not just the test someone happened to build. This chapter covers three things you need for that. The first is what the best possible test looks like. The second is how good that test can be. The third is how to measure a real test’s error rates from a finite number of trials.
The central tool is a number computed from each observation. It says how many times more likely the observation is under one distribution than under the other, and it is called the likelihood ratio. The best test compares this number with a cut-off. A stricter cut-off raises fewer false alarms but misses more real cases. Listing the best pair of error rates you can reach at every cut-off gives a curve, and that curve depends only on the two distributions. Much of what goes wrong in practice comes from summarizing the curve by one number. A single number hides how a test behaves when false alarms must be rare, and that is often the case that matters.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.2 Tests and their two errors
The chapter’s running example is a spam filter that counts suspicious words in an email. Any count above 3 is recorded as 3. The default assumption is that an email is ham, and this default is called the null hypothesis, written \(H_0\). Under it, the count has a distribution we call \(P\). We write \(p(x)\) for the probability, under \(P\), that the count equals \(x\).
The alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) is that the email is spam. Under it, the count has a distribution \(Q\), and \(q(x)\) is the probability of the count \(x\). Table 4.1 gives both distributions. Its last row is the likelihood ratio, written \(\Lambda(x) = q(x)/p(x)\), and a large ratio points to spam. Spam tends to contain more suspicious words, so the ratio grows with the count. A count of 3 is four times as likely in spam as in ham, and a count of 0 is a quarter as likely.

Divergences writes the ratio the other way up, with \(p\) on top. In this chapter the ratio always has the alternative on top.
A test is a rule that looks at the count and decides whether to say “spam”, which is called rejecting \(H_0\). The simplest test picks a set of counts and rejects exactly when the count lands in it. We will also let a test reject some counts only with some probability, by flipping a biased coin. Such a randomized test can spend a false-alarm budget exactly, as the example below shows, where a plain set of counts often cannot. We describe any test by a function \(\phi\), where \(\phi(x)\) is the probability of rejecting after seeing the count \(x\). A test that never flips a coin takes only the values 0 and 1.
A test can make two kinds of mistake. The first is to reject when the email is ham, flagging a good email as spam. This is a type I error, or false positive. Its probability is the false positive rate (FPR) of the test, written \(\alpha\).
The second mistake is to keep \(H_0\) when the email is spam, letting spam through. This is a type II error, or false negative, and its probability is written \(\beta\).
The power of a test is \(1 - \beta\), the probability that it catches spam. In classification the power is called the true positive rate (TPR), or recall.
A test has level \(\alpha\) if its FPR is at most \(\alpha\). The level is a budget, and the FPR is what the test actually spends. Both error rates are averages of \(\phi\). On a ham email the test rejects with probability \(\phi(x)\). Averaging \(\phi\) over counts drawn from \(P\), that is, summing \(\phi(x)\,p(x)\) over all counts, gives the FPR. Averaging \(\phi\) over counts drawn from \(Q\) gives the power in the same way. Take the test “reject when the count is at least 2”. Its FPR is the ham probability of the counts 2 and 3, which is \(0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3\). Its power is the spam probability of the same counts, \(0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7\). Its type II error is therefore 0.3.
The two errors pull in opposite directions. Adding a count to the rejection set adds its ham probability to the FPR and its spam probability to the power. Adding a count therefore raises the FPR and lowers the type II error, and growing the set cannot lower both. The convention treats the two errors asymmetrically. The null hypothesis is the default, and a false alarm, such as blocking a real email, is the costly error you budget for. You fix the level first, and then you look for the most powerful test at that level.
A useful yardstick is a test that ignores the email and rejects with probability \(\alpha\) by flipping a coin. It rejects ham and spam equally often, so its FPR and its power are both \(\alpha\). Any test worth using must beat it. The test that rejects only a count of 0 does not. Its FPR is 0.4, the same as a coin that rejects 40% of emails. Its power is only 0.1, while the coin’s power is 0.4. The test rejects the count most typical of ham, where spam is four times rarer.
A plain set of counts can spend only certain budgets, because each count brings its whole ham probability with it. The sets that reject every count from some cut-off upward have FPRs of 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1. Suppose your policy allows an FPR of 0.25. Rejecting only a count of 3 spends just 0.1. Adding the count 2 brings the FPR to 0.3, which overspends. The randomized test that always rejects 3, and rejects 2 with probability 0.75, spends exactly 0.25.
The randomized test is a coin flip between two plain tests. With probability 0.25 it runs “reject 3”, and otherwise it runs “reject 2 or 3”. Both error rates are averages of \(\phi\), so its errors are the same weighted average of the two tests’ errors. Its FPR is a quarter of 0.1 plus three quarters of 0.3, which is exactly 0.25. Plot each test as a point, its FPR against its type II error. Mixing tests in this way makes every point on the segment between two achievable points achievable too.
Randomization is needed only for discrete data, where moving a threshold makes the FPR jump from one count to the next. For a continuous score, moving the threshold changes the FPR smoothly, so a plain threshold can hit any budget.
Figure 4.1 shows a continuous example. A biomarker is normal with variance 1 in both groups, centred at 0 in healthy patients and at 2 in ill ones. A screening test flags patients above a threshold of 1.645, which flags 5% of healthy patients. Ill patients fall below the threshold with probability 0.361. The test therefore catches about two ill patients in three. Lowering the threshold catches more ill patients and alarms more healthy ones.






Figure 4.1: The two errors of the threshold test “reject when \(x > t\)” for \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(Q = \mathcal N(2, 1)\), with \(t\) set so that \(\alpha = 0.05\). The blue area under \(P\) beyond \(t\) is \(\alpha\); the orange area under \(Q\) before \(t\) is \(\beta = 0.361\).



Which point on the plot of FPR against type II error to pick is a policy decision. What the mathematics can say is which points are achievable at all, and the next section answers that.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.3 The Neyman–Pearson lemma
Among all tests with a given level, which one has the most power? There are infinitely many tests, one for every function \(\phi\) with values between 0 and 1. The answer is that you only need to look at one family.
The reasoning is about a budget. Rejecting a count \(x\) costs \(p(x)\) of false-positive budget, and it buys \(q(x)\) of power. The exchange rate at \(x\) is therefore \(q(x)/p(x)\), which is the likelihood ratio \(\Lambda(x)\). To get the most power for a fixed budget, spend it on the counts with the best exchange rate first. That means rejecting exactly where the likelihood ratio is above some cut-off.
A likelihood ratio (LR) test does exactly this. It picks a threshold, written \(\eta\), and rejects wherever \(q(x)\) is more than \(\eta\,p(x)\). It keeps \(H_0\) wherever \(q(x)\) is less. On ties, where the two are equal, it may reject with any probability. Writing the rule this way, rather than as a comparison of the ratio with the threshold, also handles outcomes that \(P\) never produces. At such an outcome \(p(x)\) is zero, so any positive \(q(x)\) is above \(\eta\,p(x)\) whatever the threshold. Rejecting it costs no budget at all.
The Neyman–Pearson lemma says that this family contains the best tests, in two parts. First, no test whose FPR is at most that of an LR test has a smaller type II error. Second, for every level between 0 and 1 there is an LR test whose FPR is exactly that level. To reach the level exactly, it may need to randomize on the ties. Together, the two parts say that the most powerful test at level \(\alpha\) is the LR test whose FPR is exactly \(\alpha\).
The budget picture also explains why no other test can beat it. Wherever the LR test rejects, each unit of budget buys at least \(\eta\) units of power. Wherever it keeps \(H_0\), each unit would buy at most \(\eta\). Any other test with the same budget must move some spending from counts where the ratio is above \(\eta\) to counts where it is below. Each such move gives up at least as much power as it gains.
Back to the spam filter with a budget of 0.25. The count 3 has the highest ratio, 4, and rejecting it costs 0.1. The count 2 comes next, with a ratio of 1.5. Rejecting it fully would cost another 0.2 and overspend. The cut-off therefore sits at the ratio of the count 2, which is 1.5. Counts above it are always rejected, and the count 2, tied with the cut-off, is rejected only in part. The LR test spends the remaining 0.15 on the count 2 by rejecting it with probability 0.75. This is the randomized test from Section 4.2. Its power is 0.625.
A brute-force check confirms that no other test does better. It draws 200,000 random tests, each picking every \(\phi(x)\) uniformly between 0 and 1. Of these, 11,727 stay within the budget of 0.25. The most powerful of them reaches 0.587. Figure 4.2 plots 400 random tests. Every one lies on or above the line traced by the LR tests, which the next section calls the trade-off curve.






Figure 4.2: Errors \((\alpha, \beta)\) of 400 random tests on the spam example (grey), against the curve of likelihood-ratio tests. Black dots are the deterministic thresholds, the red square is the randomized test of size 0.25, and the dotted line is the coin-flip test.



The best test looks at an observation only through its likelihood ratio. Two observations with the same ratio are interchangeable for testing, and everything else about them is noise.
Often the likelihood ratio grows with some simple statistic, such as the word count. Then “the ratio is above \(\eta\)” is the same event as “the statistic is above some threshold”. The best test is then a plain threshold on that statistic, which is why thresholding a score works. A fraud model whose score is calibrated is an example. Calibrated means that the score is the probability of fraud given the transaction. That probability grows with the likelihood ratio, as Section 4.9 shows. Thresholding a calibrated score is therefore an LR test, and no other use of the data catches more fraud at the same false-alarm rate. A score may instead rank transactions differently from the likelihood ratio. Re-ranking them by an estimate of the ratio then helps, provided the estimate puts the transactions in the same order as the true ratio.
With several independent observations, the probability of the whole sample is the product of the individual probabilities. The likelihood ratio of the sample is therefore the product of the individual ratios. The LR test thresholds its logarithm, which is a sum of independent terms. Sums of independent terms concentrate (Concentration inequalities). As the number of observations \(n\) grows, the best test can therefore make both errors small.
The Chernoff–Stein lemma makes this precise for one setting. Hold the FPR fixed at any level, and ask how fast the type II error falls as \(n\) grows. It falls like \(e^{-n\,\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)}\). Here \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of Divergences. It is the average log-ratio by which a ham observation favours ham over spam.
The Neyman–Pearson lemma needs both hypotheses to be simple. That means each one names a single, fully specified distribution. A composite hypothesis, such as “the mean is positive”, names a whole family of distributions. Each member has its own LR test, so there is usually no single test that is best against all of them at once. The main exception is a one-sided test, which asks whether a parameter such as the mean is above a given value. Suppose that for every member of the family the likelihood ratio grows with the same statistic. Then every member’s LR test is the same threshold on that statistic. That one threshold is then best against all of them.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.4 Trade-off curves
A single test gives one pair of errors. To say how hard it is to tell \(P\) from \(Q\), you want the best type II error at every level at once. For each budget \(\alpha\), look at every test whose FPR stays within it, and record the smallest type II error any of them achieves. As a function of the budget, this is the trade-off function of \(P\) and \(Q\), written \(T(\alpha)\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the LR test at each level achieves the best value. In practice you therefore compute the curve by sweeping the LR threshold.
The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of the best test plots its power against its FPR, which is \(1 - T(\alpha)\) against \(\alpha\). It holds the same information as the trade-off curve, turned upside down. A particular score, thresholded at every value, also traces an ROC curve. By the lemma, that curve lies on or below the best one.
Every trade-off curve has four properties, and each has a simple reason. It never increases, because a bigger budget still allows every test that a smaller one allowed. It lies on or below the line \(1 - \alpha\), because the coin-flip test is always available. It is convex, meaning that it bends upward like a bowl, because mixing two tests reaches every point between them. And it has no jumps. Strictly between the ends this follows from convexity. At a budget of 1 it follows from the bound \(1 - \alpha\), which forces the curve down to 0. At a budget of zero the full edition gives a separate argument.
The four properties also work in reverse. Any function with all four is the trade-off curve of some pair of distributions. So these properties are the only constraints a trade-off curve has to satisfy.
The slope of the curve has a meaning too. Moving along it means rejecting one more count with a little more probability. That spends \(p(x)\) of budget and buys \(q(x)\) of power. The curve therefore falls by the likelihood ratio \(\Lambda(x)\) for each unit the FPR rises. In other words, the slope at a point is minus the likelihood ratio at the threshold. The spam curve shows this. Its four segments in Figure 4.2 have slopes \(-4\), \(-1.5\), \(-0.667\) and \(-0.25\), which are minus the four ratios of Table 4.1. The LR test adds counts in decreasing order of their ratio, so each segment is less steep than the last. That is another way to see why the curve is convex.
The two extremes of the curve are the two extremes of difficulty. If the curve is the line \(1 - \alpha\), no test beats a coin flip, which happens exactly when \(P\) and \(Q\) are the same. If it is zero everywhere, some test makes no errors at all, which happens when the two distributions never produce the same outcome. In between, the further the curve bends below the line, the easier the problem.
One problem is harder than another if its curve is nowhere below the other’s, so that the best test misses at least as often at every budget. Two curves can cross, though. Then neither problem is harder at every level, and you have to know the level you care about.
Two more details are worth knowing. The curve’s value at \(\alpha = 0\) need not be 1. If \(Q\) puts some probability on outcomes that \(P\) never produces, a test can catch that probability with no false alarms. And the curve depends on which distribution is the null. Swapping \(P\) and \(Q\) reflects the curve across the line where the two errors are equal.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.5 The Gaussian trade-off curve
The most common pair of hypotheses in practice is a normal distribution and a shifted copy of it. A score, a biomarker or a sample mean is normal under both hypotheses, with the same spread but different centres, and its curve has a closed form.
The formula uses the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), written \(\Phi\). The value \(\Phi(x)\) is the probability that a standard normal variable is at most \(x\). Its inverse \(\Phi^{-1}\) gives the point below which a standard normal has a given probability. For example, \(\Phi^{-1}(0.95) = 1.6449\). A standard normal exceeds that point with probability 0.05.
Take \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\), the standard normal, against \(Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), the same distribution shifted right by \(\mu\). Dividing the two densities, the squared terms in \(x\) cancel, and the likelihood ratio is \(e^{\mu x - \mu^2/2}\). This grows with \(x\), so the best test is a threshold on \(x\), as in Figure 4.1. To spend a budget \(\alpha\), the threshold must leave probability \(\alpha\) of \(P\) above it. That point is \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\). The test misses when \(Q\), centred \(\mu\) higher, falls below that threshold. The curve is therefore \[T(\alpha) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu\big). \tag{4.1}\] The same curve holds for any two normal distributions with a common standard deviation. There \(\mu\) is the distance between their means, measured in standard deviations. Shifting and rescaling the observation changes no test’s errors, so only that distance matters. Figure 4.3 shows the family.






Figure 4.3: The Gaussian trade-off curve \(\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu)\) for \(\mu = 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3\). Crosses are simulated errors of threshold tests at \(\mu = 1\).



Near \(\alpha = 0\) the normal curve is vertical, because its slope is minus the likelihood ratio at the threshold. A small budget means a high threshold, and the normal likelihood ratio grows without limit as the threshold rises. The first sliver of false-alarm budget therefore buys power at an unlimited exchange rate. The Laplace pair in the next section behaves differently.
Averaging many readings makes the problem easier. Suppose you take \(n\) independent readings, each normal with the same standard deviation \(\sigma\) under both hypotheses. The alternative shifts their mean by an amount \(\delta\). Because the readings are normal with a common spread, each reading’s log likelihood ratio is a straight-line function of the reading. Their sum then depends on the data only through the sample mean, and the best test thresholds the sample mean. The sample mean has standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt n\), so the curve is Equation 4.1 with \[\mu = \frac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma}. \tag{4.2}\] How easily you can tell the two apart grows like \(\sqrt n\), the rate at which a sample mean concentrates.
For example, a monitoring job averages 100 readings and must detect a drift of \(0.2\sigma\) in the mean. The shift is then \(\mu = 2\). At a false-alarm rate of 5%, the threshold sits 1.6449 standard deviations of the sample mean above the healthy mean. The job then catches the drift with probability 0.6388. A simulation with a million draws per hypothesis agrees. Its FPR is 0.0503, and its type II error is 0.3617.

If false alarms must be rare, at a rate of \(10^{-3}\), the threshold moves out to 3.0902. The power drops to 0.1378 (Table 4.2). A strict threshold costs a lot of power when the shift is moderate.
You can also turn the question around and ask how many readings you need. Say you want power at least \(1 - \beta'\) at level \(\alpha\). The curve must then be at most \(\beta'\) at that level. The curve is \(\Phi\) evaluated at the threshold minus the shift. That value of \(\Phi\) is at most \(\beta'\) only when the threshold minus the shift is at most \(-\Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta')\). The shift must therefore be at least \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) + \Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta')\). Substituting \(\mu = \delta\sqrt n/\sigma\) and solving for \(n\) gives \[n \ge \left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) + \Phi^{-1}(1 - \beta')}{\delta/\sigma}\right)^2. \tag{4.3}\] Take a target power of 0.9 at a level of 0.01, with a drift of \(0.25\sigma\). The quantile for the level is 2.3263. The quantile for the power is 1.2816. The bound then comes to 208.3, so you need 209 readings.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.6 The Laplace trade-off curve
Replace the normal by a Laplace distribution, which has exponential tails. The Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(m, b)\) has the centre \(m\) and the scale \(b\). Its density is proportional to \(e^{-|x - m|/b}\) (Probability distributions). Take \(P = \mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) against \(Q = \mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\), a shift by \(s\). Write \(\kappa = s/b\) for the shift measured in units of the scale.
The key fact is that the likelihood ratio of this pair is capped. Moving the centre by \(s\) changes the distance from any point to the centre by at most \(s\). The exponent therefore changes by at most \(\kappa\), and the shifted density is within a factor \(e^\kappa\) of the original everywhere. The likelihood ratio stays between \(e^{-\kappa}\) and \(e^{\kappa}\). A shifted normal has no such cap, as the previous section showed.
The cap shapes the whole curve, because the slope of the curve is minus the likelihood ratio at the threshold. Above the centre \(s\) of \(Q\) the ratio sits at its cap \(e^\kappa\), and below the centre 0 of \(P\) it sits at its floor \(e^{-\kappa}\). The two ends of the curve are therefore straight lines, with slopes \(-e^{\kappa}\) and \(-e^{-\kappa}\). Between the two centres the ratio rises with \(x\), and the curve bends. The full edition derives the formula for that middle piece from the Laplace tails. The full curve is \[T(\alpha) = \begin{cases} 1 - e^{\kappa}\alpha, & \alpha < \tfrac12 e^{-\kappa}, \\[2pt] \dfrac{e^{-\kappa}}{4\alpha}, & \tfrac12 e^{-\kappa} \le \alpha \le \tfrac12, \\[6pt] e^{-\kappa}(1 - \alpha), & \alpha > \tfrac12. \end{cases} \tag{4.4}\] The three pieces correspond to a threshold above the centre of \(Q\), between the two centres, and below the centre of \(P\).
The first piece is the one that matters most. Since the ratio is never above \(e^\kappa\), no test can buy power faster than \(e^\kappa\) per unit of FPR. No test at level \(\alpha\) can therefore have power above \(e^\kappa\alpha\). For small budgets, the best test reaches exactly that power.
As an example, suppose a regression model’s residuals are roughly Laplace with scale \(b\). You suspect that a batch of inputs carries an offset equal to \(b\), so \(\kappa = 1\). The first breakpoint of the curve is then \(\tfrac12 e^{-1}\), which is 0.1839. A level of 0.05 lies below it, on the first piece, and there the best power is 0.1359. A level of 0.25 lies on the middle piece. There the type II error is \(e^{-1}\), which is 0.3679. A simulation of the threshold test with a million draws per hypothesis gives 0.3685.
To compare the two shapes fairly, match a Laplace pair and a normal pair by their best advantage. That is the largest gap between TPR and FPR that any test achieves (Section 4.7). At \(\kappa = 1\) the Laplace pair’s best advantage is 0.3935. A normal pair with \(\mu = 1.0301\) has the same. In the middle of the curve the two nearly coincide. At small levels they do not (Table 4.3).

The unbounded normal likelihood ratio lets a test find rare observations that are overwhelmingly more likely under \(Q\). The capped Laplace ratio rules that out (Figure 4.4). Two problems that look equally hard on average can therefore differ enormously when false alarms must be rare. Plan for the level you will actually use.

Right: best power on log axes. The Laplace curve follows \(e\alpha\) for small \(\alpha\); the normal curve rises far above it.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.7 Best advantage and total variation
Sometimes you want a single number for how distinguishable two distributions are. A natural choice is the advantage of a test, its TPR minus its FPR. It says how much more often the test fires under \(Q\) than under \(P\). The coin-flip test fires equally often under both, so its advantage is 0. In medicine, the advantage at a threshold is called Youden’s index.
The advantage is a sum over outcomes of \(\phi(x)\) times \(q(x) - p(x)\). Each term can be made as large as possible on its own. The best test therefore fires exactly on the outcomes where \(q\) exceeds \(p\), which is the LR test with threshold 1. Its advantage is the total amount by which \(q\) exceeds \(p\). That total is the total variation (TV) distance of Divergences. It equals half the sum of \(|q(x) - p(x)|\) over all outcomes.
Take the spam example. The gaps between the two rows of Table 4.1 are 0.3, 0.1, 0.1 and 0.3. Half their sum, the TV distance, is 0.40. Spam is more likely than ham at the counts 2 and 3, so the best test rejects those two counts. Its FPR is 0.3, and its type II error is also 0.3. Its advantage is therefore 0.4, as it should be.
For the normal pair, the best test rejects above \(\mu/2\), halfway between the means, where the two bell curves cross. Its advantage is \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\). At \(\mu = 1\) that is 0.3829. For the Laplace pair the best advantage is \(1 - e^{-\kappa/2}\). At \(\kappa = 1\) that is 0.3935.
On the trade-off curve, the advantage at level \(\alpha\) is the vertical gap between the line \(1 - \alpha\) and the curve. The gap is largest where the curve’s slope is \(-1\), which is where the LR threshold is 1 (Figure 4.5).






Figure 4.5: The Gaussian trade-off curve at \(\mu = 1\), the diagonal \(1 - \alpha\), and the advantage \(1 - \alpha - T(\alpha)\) (dashed). The red segment is the largest gap, at \(\alpha = 0.3085\), and its length is the total variation 0.3829.



The TV distance answers one question well. It tells you how small the sum of the two error rates can be, when one error counts as much as the other. That question picks out a single point of the curve, the one where the threshold is 1. It says nothing about the ends of the curve. The Laplace and normal pairs of Table 4.3 share the same TV distance, yet their powers at the smallest level differ by a factor of 36. If false alarms must be rare, the TV distance is the wrong summary, and the whole curve is the right one.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
section: 4.8 ROC summaries: why AUC hides the low-FPR regime
text:
4.8 ROC summaries: why AUC hides the low-FPR regime
Real detectors are compared on held-out data by their ROC curves. The negatives in that data are drawn under \(H_0\), and the positives under \(H_1\). The usual summary of an ROC curve is the area under the curve (AUC). In many applications only a small corner of the curve matters. A fraud team can review only a tiny fraction of transactions, and a spam filter must almost never discard real mail. Two detectors with the same AUC can differ by a factor of ten in that corner.
The AUC has a direct meaning. Write \(S_-\) for the score of a random negative and \(S_+\) for the score of a random positive, drawn independently. The AUC is the probability that \(S_+\) is above \(S_-\). In words, it is the chance that the detector ranks a random positive above a random negative.
The reason is easiest to see on a test set, by sweeping the threshold down from the top. The FPR rises by the same small step each time the threshold passes the score of a negative. At that moment, the TPR is the share of positives that score above that negative. The area under the curve adds up these TPRs, each times the same step. That is their average over the negatives, which is the chance that a positive beats a random negative. This reading assumes continuous scores, so that a positive and a negative never tie.
A common model, called the binormal model, has normal scores in both classes. Negatives score \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\). Positives score \(\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2)\), with the mean \(m\) and the standard deviation \(\sigma\). The difference of the two scores is then normal, with mean \(m\) and variance \(1 + \sigma^2\). The AUC is the chance that this difference is positive: \[\mathrm{AUC} = \Phi\big(m/\sqrt{1 + \sigma^2}\big). \tag{4.5}\] The ROC curve follows from setting the threshold from the FPR, as in Section 4.5: \[\mathrm{TPR}(\mathrm{FPR}) = 1 - \Phi\Big(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - m}{\sigma}\Big). \tag{4.6}\]
Now compare two detectors. Detector A has positives that score \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\). Detector B has positives that score \(\mathcal N(1.5811, 2^2)\), which are more spread out, with the mean chosen to give the same AUC. Both have an AUC of 0.7602. Table 4.4 shows their TPRs at two FPRs.



Table 4.4: Two detectors with normal scores in both classes and equal AUC. The simulated AUC counts correctly ranked pairs among 1,000,000.











Detector
AUC (formula / simulated)

A, \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\)

At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), detector B catches 12 times as many positives as detector A. B’s positives are more spread out, so a few of them score far above every negative. Those are exactly the cases a strict threshold catches. On linear axes the two ROC curves cross and look comparable. On log axes the gap at low FPR is obvious (Figure 4.6).






Figure 4.6: ROC curves of two detectors with the same AUC of 0.760. Left, linear axes: the curves cross and look comparable. Right, log axes: at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) detector B has 12 times the TPR of detector A.



The AUC hides this because it weighs all FPRs equally. The region of FPRs below \(10^{-3}\) is a tenth of a percent of the horizontal axis, so it barely changes the area. Most of the AUC comes from FPRs nobody would operate at.
An extreme case makes the point. Picture a detector whose ROC curve jumps to a TPR of 0.05 at an FPR of 0 and then follows the diagonal. Its AUC is only about 0.525. Yet it catches 5% of positives with no false alarms. Report the TPR at a fixed low FPR chosen by the application, and plot ROC curves on log–log axes, where that corner is visible.
For detector A, thresholding the score is already the best test. Its positives and negatives have the same spread, so its likelihood ratio grows with the score, as in Section 4.5. Detector B is different. Its positives are more spread out than its negatives, since their standard deviation is 2 against 1. Its log likelihood ratio therefore contains a positive term in the square of the score, and the ratio is large at both ends. The best test for B would also flag very low scores. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, B’s best ROC curve is at least as good as the one plotted.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.9 The Bayesian view
The Neyman–Pearson lemma uses no prior. But often you know a base rate, such as 1% of patients being ill or one transaction in a thousand being fraud. Then the useful question is how likely \(H_1\) is, given the observation. The likelihood ratio answers it with one multiplication.
Write \(\pi\) for the base rate, the probability of \(H_1\) before seeing anything. The odds of \(H_1\) are its probability divided by the probability of \(H_0\). Bayes’ rule says that the odds after seeing \(x\) are the odds before, multiplied by the likelihood ratio: \[\frac{\Pr[H_1 \mid x]}{\Pr[H_0 \mid x]} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} \times \Lambda(x). \tag{4.7}\] To see why, note that the chance that \(H_1\) holds and you see \(x\) is \(\pi\,q(x)\). The chance that \(H_0\) holds and you see \(x\) is \((1 - \pi)\,p(x)\). Dividing each by the total chance of seeing \(x\) gives the two posterior probabilities. That total cancels in their ratio.
The rule also tells you how to decide. To make as few mistakes as possible, say \(H_1\) whenever its posterior odds exceed 1. That happens exactly when \(\Lambda(x)\) is above \((1 - \pi)/\pi\). The decision with the fewest errors is therefore again an LR test, with its threshold set by the base rate.
Unequal costs change only the threshold. If a miss costs \(c\) times as much as a false alarm, the threshold becomes \((1 - \pi)/(c\pi)\). The test then moves along the same trade-off curve.
When both hypotheses are equally likely beforehand, the fewest errors means the smallest sum of the two error rates. Minimizing that sum is the same as maximizing the advantage. Take one minus the TV distance, and halve the result. That is the smallest possible probability of error. For the normal pair at \(\mu = 1\), it is 0.3085.
The same rule applies to any evidence, not only to the raw observation. If all you know is that the test fired, the likelihood ratio of that event is the chance of firing under \(H_1\) divided by the chance under \(H_0\). That is the TPR divided by the FPR.
Take the biomarker test with \(\mu = 2\) in a population where 1% are ill. At an FPR of 0.05 the power is 0.6388. A positive result is then 12.8 times as likely in an ill patient as in a healthy one. Even so, a positive patient is ill with probability only 0.114, so nine in ten positives are false alarms. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) the power is 0.1378. A positive result is then 137.8 times as likely in an ill patient. A positive patient is ill with probability 0.582 (Figure 4.7).






Figure 4.7: Posterior probability of illness after a positive result, as a function of the prior, for the \(\mu = 2\) biomarker test at two thresholds. At 1% prevalence (dashed line) the stricter test gives 0.582 against 0.114.



The stricter threshold catches fewer ill patients, but it makes each positive result far more informative. This is a second reason that behaviour at low FPR matters. When positives are rare, the FPR, not the power, decides whether an alarm is worth acting on.
The test with the fewest errors at this base rate is stricter still. It rejects when the ratio exceeds 99. For this pair, that means a reading above 3.2976. Its FPR is \(4.88\times10^{-4}\). Its power is only 0.0972. When both kinds of error count equally and the disease is rare, it is cheapest to rarely say “ill”.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.10 Measuring rates from finite trials
Everything so far assumed that you know \(P\) and \(Q\). In practice you measure a detector’s FPR on test data, where you count the false positives among the negatives. Write \(n\) for the number of negatives and \(k\) for the number of false positives among them. If each negative is falsely flagged independently, with the same probability \(\alpha\), then \(k\) follows a binomial distribution (Probability distributions). The intervals below are computed from that distribution, so they are only as valid as this model.
The measured rate \(k/n\) is uncertain, and at low rates the uncertainty is large compared with the rate itself. When the rate is small, a count of \(k\) events fluctuates by about \(\sqrt k\). Its relative uncertainty is then about \(1/\sqrt k\). The relative precision of a measured rate therefore depends mainly on how many events you see, not on \(n\) alone.
The Clopper–Pearson interval turns the observed count into a range of plausible true rates. It asks which true rates would make the observed count unsurprising. A true rate far above \(k/n\) would make a count as small as \(k\) very unlikely. The upper end \(u\) is therefore the rate at which seeing \(k\) or fewer events has a small probability. Likewise, the lower end \(l\) is the rate at which seeing \(k\) or more events has that small probability.
For a two-sided interval at confidence \(1 - a\), each end gets half of the allowed failure probability \(a\). The two ends solve \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, l) \ge k] = \frac a2, \qquad \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = \frac a2. \tag{4.8}\] By convention, the lower end is 0 when no events are seen, and the upper end is 1 when every trial is an event. The interval contains the true rate with probability at least \(1 - a\).
The reason is that each end can miss on only one side. The true rate lies above the upper end only when the observed count was unusually small for it. By the choice of \(u\), that happens with probability at most \(a/2\). The same holds for the lower end. The union bound, which says that the chance of either of two events is at most the sum of their chances, then gives at most \(a\) in total.
The interval is called exact because it uses the binomial distribution itself, not an approximation. It is also conservative, because its coverage is at least \(1 - a\) and often more. A simulation checks this, with a true FPR of \(10^{-3}\) and 10,000 negatives. Over 2,000 runs, the 95% interval covered the true rate 97.20% of the time.
Often you need only an upper bound, for example to claim that an FPR is below a target. The upper end on its own misses with probability at most \(a/2\). The upper end of a two-sided interval at confidence \(1 - a\) is therefore a one-sided upper bound at confidence \(1 - a/2\). A two-sided 90% interval gives each end a failure probability of 0.05. Its upper end is therefore a one-sided 95% upper bound. You compute it by solving \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = 0.05\). For 1 false positive in 1,000 negatives, this bound is 0.0047 (the code below prints it).
With no events at all, the chance of seeing none at rate \(u\) is \((1 - u)^n\). The one-sided 95% upper bound solves \((1 - u)^n = 0.05\). For a small rate, \((1 - u)^n\) is close to \(e^{-nu}\), so the bound is about \(\ln(20)/n\). Since \(\ln 20\) is about 3, the bound is about \(3/n\), a shortcut called the rule of three. With 3,000 negatives and no false positives, the bound is \(9.981\times10^{-4}\). Turned around, certifying an FPR below \(10^{-3}\) at 95% confidence takes 2,995 negatives with no false positive at all.
Here is what this means for the monitor with \(\mu = 2\), run at its \(10^{-3}\) threshold. Its true FPR is \(10^{-3}\), and its true TPR is 0.1378. Test it on 10,000 negatives and 10,000 positives. Table 4.5 shows one simulated run.



Table 4.5: One simulated evaluation of the \(\mu = 2\) test at its \(10^{-3}\) threshold, with 10,000 examples per class.





Quantity
Count
Estimate
95% Clopper–Pearson interval




False positives

True positives

The TPR is pinned down to about \(\pm 0.007\). The FPR is not, because it rests on only 10 events. The data are consistent with a true FPR anywhere from about half to almost twice the target. With 100,000 negatives you would expect about 100 false positives. The interval would then be \([0.00081, 0.00122]\), about 20% on either side. This gives a rule of thumb. You need on the order of \(100/\alpha\) negatives to measure an FPR of \(\alpha\) to within a factor of about 1.2. Figure 4.8 shows how slowly the interval tightens as the number of negatives grows.






Figure 4.8: 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals for an observed false-positive rate of exactly \(10^{-3}\), as the number of negatives grows from \(10^3\) to \(10^6\), with the upper end of the two-sided Hoeffding interval for comparison.



Two other common intervals do worse on the same 10 false positives. The Wald interval uses a normal approximation to the binomial. Here it gives \([0.00038, 0.00162]\), which is too narrow. It is also symmetric, while a count of rare events is skewed to the right. And with no events it collapses to \([0, 0]\), claiming certainty from no data.
The Hoeffding interval comes from Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration inequalities). That inequality uses only the fact that each outcome lies between 0 and 1. It therefore assumes the largest variance such an outcome can have, a quarter, while the true variance of a rare false positive is tiny. Here its half-width is 0.0136, more than 13 times the rate being measured.
One last trap is that the threshold is often estimated too. Suppose you choose the threshold on the same data so that the measured FPR is \(10^{-3}\). The choice favours thresholds whose measured FPR happens to be low by chance. The chosen threshold therefore looks better on that data than it is, and its true FPR is as uncertain as the interval above. Choose thresholds on one split of the data, and measure their rates on another.

title: 4  Hypothesis testing
text:
4.11 Code
The normal trade-off curve and the Clopper–Pearson interval need only the standard library. The quantile is found by bisection on the upper tail, which keeps full precision when \(\alpha\) is tiny. Computing \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\) directly would round \(1 - \alpha\) to a number very close to 1 and lose the digits that matter.
from collections.abc import Callable
from math import erfc, exp, lgamma, log, log1p, sqrt


def normal_cdf(x: float) -> float:
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def upper_quantile(a: float) -> float:
    """The point a standard normal exceeds with probability a, found by bisection on the tail."""
    lo, hi = -40.0, 40.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if 0.5 * erfc(mid / sqrt(2)) > a else (lo, mid)
    return lo


def gaussian_power(alpha: float, mu: float) -> float:
    """Best power at false positive rate alpha between N(0, 1) and N(mu, 1)."""
    return 1 - normal_cdf(upper_quantile(alpha) - mu)


def binom_cdf(k: int, n: int, p: float) -> float:
    """Pr[Binomial(n, p) <= k], summed in log space."""
    if p <= 0.0:
        return 1.0
    if p >= 1.0:
        return 1.0 if k >= n else 0.0
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(k + 1):
        log_pmf = lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(i + 1) - lgamma(n - i + 1) + i * log(p) + (n - i) * log1p(-p)
        total += exp(log_pmf)
    return total


def clopper_pearson(k: int, n: int, confidence: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Exact two-sided interval for a rate after k successes in n trials."""
    tail = (1 - confidence) / 2  # a/2 in the text

    def solve(f: Callable[[float], float], target: float) -> float:
        """The rate p at which f, a binomial CDF that falls as p grows, equals target."""
        lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0
        for _ in range(100):
            mid = (lo + hi) / 2
            lo, hi = (mid, hi) if f(mid) > target else (lo, mid)
        return lo

    # Lower end: Pr[Bin(n, l) >= k] = tail, that is Pr[Bin(n, l) <= k - 1] = 1 - tail.
    lower = 0.0 if k == 0 else solve(lambda p: binom_cdf(k - 1, n, p), 1 - tail)
    # Upper end: Pr[Bin(n, u) <= k] = tail.
    upper = 1.0 if k == n else solve(lambda p: binom_cdf(k, n, p), tail)
    return lower, upper


def upper_bound(k: int, n: int, confidence: float = 0.95) -> float:
    """One-sided upper bound: the upper end of the two-sided interval at confidence 2 * confidence - 1."""
    return clopper_pearson(k, n, 2 * confidence - 1)[1]


print(f"{gaussian_power(0.05, 2.0):.4f} {gaussian_power(1e-3, 2.0):.4f}")  # 0.6388 0.1378
low, high = clopper_pearson(10, 10_000)
print(f"[{low:.5f}, {high:.5f}]")  # [0.00048, 0.00184]
print(f"{upper_bound(1, 1_000):.4f}")  # 0.0047
print(f"{upper_bound(0, 3_000):.3e}")  # 9.981e-04
The last two lines are one-sided 95% upper bounds. The first is for 1 false positive in 1,000 negatives. The second is for no false positives in 3,000, close to the rule of three’s \(3/n\).

text:
4.12 Cheat sheet



Table 4.6: The results of this chapter.









Result
Statement




Errors of a test \(\phi\)
FPR \(\alpha\) is the average of \(\phi\) under \(P\); power \(1 - \beta\) (TPR) is its average under \(Q\)


Neyman–Pearson
The LR test, rejecting where \(q > \eta p\) and randomizing at ties, is most powerful at its level


Trade-off curve \(T(\alpha)\)
Best \(\beta\) at level \(\alpha\); non-increasing, at most \(1 - \alpha\), convex, continuous; slope \(-\Lambda\) at the threshold


Normal shift \(\mu\)
\(T(\alpha) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu)\); \(n\) averaged readings: \(\mu = \delta\sqrt n/\sigma\)


Laplace shift \(\kappa = s/b\)
Equation 4.4; power at most \(e^\kappa\alpha\)


Best advantage
\(\max(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}) = \mathrm{TV}\); normal \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\), Laplace \(1 - e^{-\kappa/2}\)


AUC
\(\Pr[S_+ > S_-]\); binormal \(\Phi(m/\sqrt{1 + \sigma^2})\)


Bayes
Posterior odds \(=\) prior odds \(\times\,\Lambda\); an alarm has \(\Lambda = \mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR}\)


Clopper–Pearson
\(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, l) \ge k] = \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = a/2\)


One-sided upper bound
95% one-sided \(=\) upper end of the two-sided 90% interval; zero events: \(u \approx 3/n\)






Rules of thumb

To find the best test, compute the likelihood ratio and threshold it. If the ratio grows with a statistic, threshold the statistic.
Compare detectors by their TPR at a fixed low FPR, on log axes. AUC and TV hide that regime.
A capped likelihood ratio caps power at small levels: power is at most the cap times \(\alpha\).
To measure a rate near \(\alpha\), plan for about \(100/\alpha\) trials, and report a Clopper–Pearson interval.
