The rows \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 0)\) are mirror images. Each holds the same two values as the other, with the example and the fresh copy exchanged. In these two rows the test and renamed columns differ. The renamed column holds the test column’s values with the two mirror-image rows swapped. Those rows have the same probability, 0.21, so the averages agree.
The renaming needs one condition. The two points must be interchangeable, which holds when they are drawn independently from the same distribution. If \(z_1'\) came from a different distribution, the two mirror-image rows would have different probabilities. The averages would then differ, and the identity would fail.
To bound the gap, bound each term of Equation 7.1. An algorithm is \(\beta\)-uniformly stable if replacing any one training example by any other moves the loss of the trained model by at most \(\beta\), at every test point. The bound must hold in the worst case, for every training set, every replacement and every test point. The number \(\beta\) often shrinks as \(n\) grows, since each example then carries less weight. For a randomized algorithm such as SGD, the condition applies to the loss averaged over the algorithm’s own randomness.
Figure 7.1 shows the definition at work. One label is flipped, and the fitted model moves a lot under weak regularization and barely under strong regularization.






Figure 7.1: One-dimensional logistic regression trained on 30 points, on \(S\) and on \(S^{(i)}\), where the positive example with the largest feature value is replaced by the same point with its label flipped. Left: \(\lambda = 0.01\). Right: \(\lambda = 1\). The titles compare the change in the weight with the bound \(2L/(\lambda n)\) of Section 7.5.



If the algorithm is \(\beta\)-uniformly stable, every term in the brackets lies between \(-\beta\) and \(\beta\) (for a randomized algorithm, once averaged over its randomness). So does their average, and the expected gap is at most \(\beta\) in size: \[\big|\mathbb E[\mathrm{gap}]\big| \le \beta. \tag{7.2}\] What makes this bound useful is what it leaves out. No set of models appears in it, so it holds for any algorithm, however rich the set of models it could output. This is why stability gives guarantees for SGD on large models, where measuring that richness gives nothing useful.
The price is that uniform stability is a worst case. The identity averages over examples and data, while \(\beta\) takes the worst training set, the worst replacement and the worst test point. So \(\beta\) can be far above the true gap. Weaker notions of stability that use averages also exist (Bousquet & Elisseeff 2002).
At the opposite end from a stable algorithm sits a memorizing lookup table. It stores the training set and predicts the stored label at a training point and \(+1\) everywhere else. Score it with the 0-1 loss, which is 1 for a wrong prediction and 0 for a right one. With continuous features, a fresh point almost surely misses the table and gets the prediction \(+1\). In the running example half the labels are \(-1\), so the test error is one half, while the training error is 0, for every \(n\).
Now take a training example whose label is \(-1\), and replace it by a point elsewhere. The table no longer stores the old point, so the prediction there falls back to \(+1\). Tested on the old example, the loss jumps from 0 to 1, so \(\beta = 1\). The gap of one half obeys the bound but never shrinks.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.4 High probability: the Bousquet–Elisseeff bound
Equation 7.2 controls the gap on average over training sets. But you train once, on one training set, so you need the gap of your model to be small with high probability. The tool for that is McDiarmid’s inequality from Concentration inequalities. It says that a function of many independent inputs stays close to its average if none of the inputs can move it by much. The chance of a large deviation falls exponentially in the square of its size.
The gap is such a function. It depends on \(n\) independent examples, and uniform stability limits how much one example can move it. Replacing an example moves the test loss by at most \(\beta\), because it moves the loss at every point by at most \(\beta\).
It also moves the training loss, and this is where a second condition enters. The training loss is an average of \(n\) terms, one per example. For the other examples, the term is evaluated at the same point under two models, and stability limits its change. The replaced example’s own term is different. Before the replacement it is a loss at \(z_i\), and after it a loss at \(z_i'\), two different points. Stability compares two models at the same point, so it says nothing about this term. Only a bound on the loss itself limits it. So the result assumes that every loss lies between 0 and a maximum \(M\). Without such a bound, one example could move the training loss by any amount, and McDiarmid’s inequality would not apply.
Write \(\delta\) for the failure probability, the chance that the guarantee does not hold. Suppose the algorithm is \(\beta\)-uniformly stable and the loss lies between 0 and \(M\). Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over the training set, \[R(A(S)) \le \hat R_S(A(S)) + \beta + (2n\beta + M)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}. \tag{7.3}\] This is the bound of Bousquet & Elisseeff (2002). They define stability by removing an example rather than replacing it, and the form above restates their bound for replacement. The same argument applied to the gap with its sign reversed gives a matching lower bound.
The bound adds two things to the training loss you observe. The first is \(\beta\), the bound on the expected gap. The second is a deviation term, which says how far one training set can stray from the average. Together they make up the bound’s width. Inside the deviation term, the part with \(M\) is what Hoeffding’s inequality gives for a single fixed model. That model’s training loss is an average of \(n\) independent losses between 0 and \(M\). Call it the fixed-model term. It falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), and you pay it even without any learning.
The part with \(2n\beta\) is the price of learning. Multiplied out, it equals \(\beta\sqrt{2n\ln(1/\delta)}\), so it goes to zero only if \(\beta\) shrinks faster than \(1/\sqrt n\) as the training set grows. Figure 7.2 shows three cases. When \(\beta\) falls like \(1/n\), as for regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) below, the width falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). That is only a constant factor above the fixed-model term. When \(\beta\) falls like \(n^{-3/4}\), the width still falls, but only like \(n^{-1/4}\). And when \(\beta\) falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), the width does not fall at all. The bound is then useless, although Equation 7.2 still says the expected gap is at most \(\beta\).






Figure 7.2: Width of the high-probability bound, Equation 7.3, with \(M = 1\) and \(\delta = 0.05\), for stability \(\beta = 1/n\), \(n^{-3/4}\) and \(n^{-1/2}\), against the Hoeffding width for a single fixed model.



The bound is loose because McDiarmid’s inequality charges every example the full worst case, while in reality the effects of different examples largely cancel. Later work removed most of this slack. Feldman & Vondrák (2018) proved a bound that is useful whenever \(\beta\) goes to zero, at any rate. Two later papers went further for losses between 0 and 1 (Feldman & Vondrák 2019; Bousquet, Klochkov & Zhivotovskiy 2020). Their bound is \(\beta\), multiplied by logarithmic factors, plus the fixed-model term. With it, a \(\beta\) of order \(1/\sqrt n\) also gives a gap of order \(1/\sqrt n\), up to logarithmic factors.
For a sense of scale, apply Equation 7.3 to regularized logistic regression with 10,000 examples and \(\delta = 0.05\). The features have size 1, and the next section shows that \(\beta\) is then \(2/(\lambda n)\). The logistic loss has no upper limit in general, since it grows as a prediction gets more confidently wrong. Here it is bounded because the penalty keeps the weights at size at most \(1/\lambda\), as the next section also shows. With features of size 1, no prediction can then be more wrong than \(1/\lambda\) allows, and the largest loss \(M\) is \(\ln(1 + e^{1/\lambda})\). That is 1.313 for \(\lambda = 1\) and 10.000 for \(\lambda = 0.1\).
With \(\lambda = 1\), the bound adds 0.065 to the training loss. With \(\lambda = 0.1\), it adds 0.614. In both cases the stability term \(2n\beta\) makes up three quarters or more of the width. The expected gap itself is far smaller. Take \(\lambda = 1\). Already with 1,000 examples, a tenth as many, the expected gap is \(2.53\times10^{-4}\), and it keeps falling like \(1/n\).

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.5 Regularized ERM is stable
The bounds above need an algorithm with small \(\beta\). The first such algorithm is regularized ERM, which covers ridge regression, regularized logistic regression and support vector machines. It picks the weights \(w_S\) that minimize the training loss plus a penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\) on the size of the weights.
Stability gives a new reading of the regularizer. With a convex loss, the penalty makes the objective a bowl whose curvature is at least \(\lambda\) everywhere. Replacing one example changes only one term of the objective, and that term carries weight \(1/n\). A small change can only tilt a steep bowl a little, so the bottom of the bowl moves only a little.
Two properties of the loss turn this picture into a number, and Optimization defines both. A loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz when its gradient never exceeds \(L\) in size. Then moving the weights by some distance changes the loss by at most \(L\) times that distance. A loss is convex when its curvature is never negative. If the loss is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz for every example, then replacing one example moves the minimizer by at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\). The loss at every test point then moves by at most \(L\) times that, which gives \[\beta = \frac{2L^2}{\lambda n}. \tag{7.4}\]
Each condition has a job. The Lipschitz bound limits how hard the one changed term can tilt the bowl, since its gradient changes by at most \(2L/n\). It also turns a movement of the weights into a change of the loss. Convexity of the loss keeps the whole objective a bowl with curvature at least \(\lambda\). Without it, the data term can cancel the curvature of the penalty. Optimization shows a non-convex loss with two valleys where flipping one label makes the minimizer jump from one valley to the other, however large \(n\) is. Squared loss is convex but not Lipschitz everywhere. When the features and labels are bounded, you can still use the result for ridge regression. The minimizer then lies in a bounded region, and the squared loss is Lipschitz there.
The same reasoning bounds the size of the weights. At the minimizer the gradient of the objective is zero. Setting it to zero says that \(\lambda w_S\) equals minus the average gradient of the losses. That average has size at most \(L\), so \(\|w_S\|\) is at most \(L/\lambda\). With bounded features this also bounds every prediction, which is how the previous section found the largest loss \(M\) of regularized logistic regression.
Because \(\beta\) falls like \(1/n\), faster than \(1/\sqrt n\), both the expected-gap and the high-probability bounds go to zero as the training set grows. Regularization buys stability linearly, since doubling \(\lambda\) halves \(\beta\). But it is not free, because a larger \(\lambda\) also pulls the weights towards zero and away from the best fit. So the test loss is U-shaped in \(\lambda\), and too little regularization overfits while too much underfits.
The running example tests the bound. The gradient of the logistic loss is the feature vector scaled by a probability, a number between 0 and 1. With features of size 1 its size is at most 1, so the loss is 1-Lipschitz and \(\beta = 2/(\lambda n)\). The script fits the model on \(S\) and then on \(S^{(i)}\) for 10 random examples, each replaced by the same point with its label flipped. It records the largest change in the weights and in the loss. To find the test point where the loss changes most, it checks 2,000 random test points and the points that lie in the direction the weights moved.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.6 SGD is stable if you stop early
text:
7.6 SGD is stable if you stop early
Large models are not trained to an exact minimizer but by SGD, for a number of steps. At each step, SGD picks one training example uniformly at random and moves the weights against the gradient of its loss, scaled by a step size \(\eta_t\). The sum of the step sizes over all steps is the total step size. Hardt, Recht & Singer (2016) showed that SGD itself is stable, with a \(\beta\) that grows with the total step size. This turns “train for fewer epochs” into a guarantee.
The idea is to run SGD twice, once on \(S\) and once on \(S^{(i)}\), with the same starting point and the same sequence of random picks. Sharing the picks is allowed, because stability compares the average loss of each run, and sharing does not change either average. The two runs can then drift apart only on the steps that pick example \(i\), because only there do they step on different examples.
The other steps must not push the runs apart, and this needs three conditions. The loss must be convex, because on a non-convex loss a gradient step can push two points apart. It must also be \(\rho\)-smooth, meaning that its gradient changes by at most a constant \(\rho\) per unit of distance. (Optimization writes this constant as \(\beta\), but here \(\beta\) is the stability.) And every step size must be at most \(2/\rho\), for the reason the next paragraph shows. Under these conditions, a gradient step on the same loss never moves two points farther apart than they were.
A one-dimensional loss shows why the step size matters. For the parabola \(\frac\rho2w^2\), a gradient step with step size \(\eta\) multiplies every distance by \(|1 - \eta\rho|\). That factor is at most 1 exactly when \(\eta\) is at most \(2/\rho\). A larger step overshoots the minimum and blows differences up.
The steps that pick example \(i\) need a fourth condition. The loss must be \(L\)-Lipschitz, so that its gradient has size at most \(L\). Such a step moves each run by at most \(\eta_t L\), so it pushes the runs apart by at most \(2L\eta_t\). Because the picks are uniform, it happens with probability \(1/n\), and on average the distance grows by at most \(2L\eta_t/n\) per step. Many implementations instead shuffle the data once per epoch, and the argument as stated does not cover them. Adding up the steps and multiplying by \(L\) to turn distance into loss gives \[\beta \le \frac{2L^2}{n}\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t, \tag{7.5}\] where \(T\) is the number of steps. The bound holds on average over the random picks.
Figure 7.4 shows this as a staircase. A single run jumps when example \(i\) is picked, which happens about once per epoch, and otherwise does not grow. In practice, a gradient step on a curved loss often brings two points closer together, so single runs also shrink between jumps.






Figure 7.4: Distance between coupled SGD runs on \(S\) and \(S^{(1)}\) (\(n = 100\), \(\eta = 0.25\)), for three single runs and the average over 200 runs, against the bound \((2L/n)\sum_t\eta_t\). Single runs jump when example 1 is drawn and contract otherwise. Dotted lines mark epochs.



Stability therefore degrades with training time. Take a constant step \(\eta\), and train for a number of epochs \(E\), which is \(En\) steps. The total step size is \(\eta En\), and Equation 7.5 becomes \(\beta \le 2L^2\eta E\). The \(n\) cancels, so for a fixed number of epochs, more data does not improve the bound. One pass over the data gives \(\beta \le 2L^2\eta\).
This makes early stopping a trade-off rather than a trick. Training longer lowers the optimization error, the excess of the training loss over that of the best weights. But it raises \(\beta\), and the excess test loss pays for both. Take averaged SGD, which outputs the average of the weights along the way rather than the last ones. For convex Lipschitz losses, its optimization error falls like one over the total step size \(\eta T\). The stability bound, in contrast, grows like \(\eta T/n\). Balancing the two puts the best total step size at order \(\sqrt n\). There the bound on the expected excess test loss falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), plus a term proportional to the step size. Training much longer buys optimization accuracy that the growing stability term gives back.
The running example shows the trade-off without regularization. It uses 100 examples and a constant step \(\eta = 0.25\). The logistic loss with features of size 1 is \(\frac14\)-smooth, so the condition \(\eta \le 8\) holds. With \(L = 1\) the loss bound is \(0.5E\). The script averages over 100 pairs of runs, with the first example replaced by a fresh draw.

The size of the bound, however, is far off. After one epoch the bound is 14 times the measured gap, and after 40 epochs it is 165 times. The reason is that the argument uses only the fact that a step does not push points apart. The distance between the runs actually levels off near 0.4, while the bound grows linearly.
Convexity is the condition that fails for neural networks. On a non-convex loss, a gradient step can push two points apart. Hardt, Recht & Singer still get a bound in that case, but it grows polynomially in the number of steps rather than linearly in the total step size.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.7 An unstable algorithm: 1-nearest neighbour
Seeing an algorithm without stability makes clear what stability rules out. The nearest neighbour (NN) rule with one neighbour, 1-NN, predicts the label of the closest training point. It fits every training example using that example itself, which is exactly the dependence that stability forbids.
Its training error is 0, since each training point is its own nearest neighbour when the points are distinct. Its \(\beta\) under the 0-1 loss is 1, the largest possible value. To see this, replace a training example by the same point with the opposite label. The prediction at that point flips, and the loss there changes from 0 to 1.
Its gap does not close when the labels are noisy. Write \(p(x)\) for the probability that the label at the point \(x\) is \(+1\). As the training set grows, the nearest neighbour of a test point lies almost on top of it. Its label is then an independent draw with the same probability \(p(x)\). The two labels disagree with probability \(2p(x)(1 - p(x))\), and the average of this over \(x\) is the limit of the test error (Cover & Hart 1967). Since the training error is 0, this limit is also the limit of the gap.
1-NN is still a reasonable classifier. The best possible classifier, the Bayes classifier, predicts the more likely label at each point, and the limiting error of 1-NN is at most twice its error. But the training error of 1-NN says nothing about how close it gets to that best error. With a majority vote over more neighbours, a prediction rarely changes when one example is replaced. Its uniform stability is still \(\beta = 1\), though, because replacing one neighbour can flip a vote that is split as evenly as possible. Average-case notions of stability explain it (Devroye & Wagner 1979).
In the running example the best possible error is 0.250, and the 1-NN limit is 0.338. Table 7.5 compares 1-NN with the regularized logistic regression, averaging over 10 training sets and measuring the 0-1 error on 2,000 test points.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.8 Overfitting is memorization of individual examples
text:
7.8 Overfitting is memorization of individual examples
The identity of Section 7.3 says which examples carry the gap. Each term of Equation 7.1 is the self-influence, or memorization score, of one example. It is the example’s loss under the model trained without it, minus its loss under the model trained with it: \[\mathrm{mem}_i(S) = \ell\big(A(S^{(i)}), z_i\big) - \ell\big(A(S), z_i\big). \tag{7.6}\] The expected gap is the average of these scores. Each score can be measured directly, by retraining with the example replaced. Feldman (2020) uses the same idea with accuracy in place of loss and with the example removed rather than replaced.
The script checks the identity on training sets of 40 examples. It fits the model, then for each example replaces it by a fresh draw, refits, and records the score. It repeats this over 100 training sets and reports each average with its standard error, written after a ± sign. At \(\lambda = 0.01\) the measured gap is \(0.1482 \pm 0.0073\). The average self-influence is \(0.1422 \pm 0.0025\). At \(\lambda = 0.1\) the two are \(0.0420 \pm 0.0017\) and \(0.0416 \pm 0.0003\). They agree within their errors, as the identity requires.
The scores are uneven, and the reason is redundancy. A typical example is fitted well whether or not it is in the training set, because its neighbours carry the same information. An atypical example, such as a mislabelled point or a member of a rare subgroup, is fitted only if it is there itself. So the atypical examples carry most of the gap.
The running example makes this visible. About a quarter of the examples have a label that goes against the trend. At \(\lambda = 0.01\), their average self-influence is 0.284, three times the 0.097 of the other examples. At \(\lambda = 0.1\) the two are 0.055 and 0.037. Regularization flattens the profile, because it limits how far any one example can pull the weights, and atypical examples pull hardest (Figure 7.7).






Figure 7.7: Self-influence \(\ell(w(S^{(i)}), z_i) - \ell(w(S), z_i)\) of each training example against \(y_ix_{i1}\), which measures how typical its label is, for \(n = 40\) and two values of \(\lambda\). Examples whose label goes against the trend have the largest self-influence. The dashed line is the average, which equals the expected gap.



A small average leaves room for a few heavily memorized examples. The expected gap needs only the average score to be small. Uniform stability is a stronger requirement, because it caps every score at \(\beta\).
Memorization is not always a defect. Feldman (2020) shows that it can be necessary when the data have a long tail of rare subpopulations, each seen about once. On such data, an algorithm that does not memorize those rare examples loses accuracy on the tail. So a large gap can come with good test accuracy. The empirical evidence points the same way. Zhang et al. (2017) found that deep networks fit even randomly relabelled training data perfectly. Feldman & Zhang (2020) measured memorization scores on image benchmarks and found the highest scores on atypical and mislabelled examples. In practice, expect the rarest examples to be the most memorized, and measure them rather than only the average.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.9 Code
There is no snippet, because every number here comes from retraining models. The full edition’s script stability.py runs every experiment and draws every figure in this chapter. Run it from the repository root.
uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/stability.py
Its results support four lessons. The \(1/(\lambda n)\) scaling of regularized ERM holds, but the measured changes and gaps sit between 4 and more than 30 times below the bound. The gap identity, unlike the bounds, is exact. The SGD bound gets the direction right and the size wrong. And 1-NN has training error 0 and test error 0.35, while the training and test errors of regularized logistic regression meet.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.1 Why this matters
Some computations must hide something, such as the message in an encrypted file, or a value split among several holders that no single holder may learn. To build or review such a system, you need a precise answer to one question. What does it mean that an observer learns nothing it was not supposed to learn?
Against unlimited computing power, a key shorter than the message cannot hide it perfectly, because seeing the ciphertext rules some messages out. Perfect hiding is possible, but it needs a key as long as all the data. Practical cryptography therefore asks for less, namely that every attacker with realistic computing power learns almost nothing. This chapter makes “realistic” and “almost nothing” precise, and shows the few tools that prove such statements.
The whole subject rests on one idea, which is that security is a game. A challenger secretly flips a fair coin to pick one of two worlds, for example one world where it encrypts one message and one where it encrypts another. The challenger shows the result to an adversary, whose task is to guess which world it is in. An adversary who learns nothing from what it sees is right half the time, whatever it answers, so only a win rate above one half shows that something leaked. A scheme is secure when no efficient adversary beats the coin by more than a tiny amount, where “efficient” means roughly “feasible in practice” and is defined below. Proofs reach that conclusion in small steps, each of which changes one thing in what the adversary sees, and the rest of the chapter shows how.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.2 Advantage
The simplest adversary sees one sample and answers with a single bit, and it is called a distinguisher, written \(A\). Read its answer 1 as “I think this sample came from the second world”. Let \(X\) be the distribution of the sample in the first world, and let \(Y\) be its distribution in the second. A distinguisher that is any good says 1 more often on samples from \(Y\) than on samples from \(X\). Its advantage is the gap between how often it says 1 in the two worlds. In symbols, write \(\Pr[A(X) = 1]\) for the probability that it says 1 when its sample comes from \(X\), and likewise for \(Y\). Then \[\mathrm{Adv}_A(X, Y) = \big|\Pr[A(X) = 1] - \Pr[A(Y) = 1]\big|. \tag{8.1}\]
The absolute value also credits a distinguisher whose answers point the wrong way, since flipping its answers turns it into one that points the right way. A distinguisher that ignores its sample says 1 equally often in both worlds, so its advantage is 0. One that is always right has advantage 1.
The advantage and the chance of winning the coin game measure the same thing. The distinguisher wins when it says 1 in the second world or 0 in the first. Each world comes up half the time, so its chance of winning is the average of these two success rates: \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \tfrac12\Pr[A(Y) = 1] + \tfrac12\Pr[A(X) = 0] = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\big(\Pr[A(Y) = 1] - \Pr[A(X) = 1]\big). \tag{8.2}\] So a distinguisher whose answer 1 points to the second world wins with probability one half plus half its advantage. For example, let the first world be a fair coin and the second a coin that lands heads with probability 0.6. A distinguisher that says 1 on heads says 1 with probability 0.6 in the second world and 0.5 in the first. Its advantage is therefore 0.1. It wins the game with probability 0.55, which is one half plus 0.05.
You already know distinguishers from machine learning. A classifier trained to tell real images from generated ones is a distinguisher. If it outputs 1 for “real”, it says 1 on real images at its true positive rate and on generated images at its false positive rate. Its advantage is the difference between the two rates. Deciding which of two distributions produced a sample is a hypothesis test, the subject of Hypothesis testing.
How large can the advantage be? Some outcomes are more likely under one distribution than under the other. A distinguisher, even a randomized one, can only choose for each outcome how often to say 1 on it. Saying 1 on an outcome that is more likely under \(Y\) widens the gap, and saying 1 on one that is more likely under \(X\) narrows it. So the best distinguisher says 1 exactly on the outcomes that are more likely under \(Y\), however long it may run. Its advantage is the extra probability that \(Y\) puts on those outcomes, compared with \(X\). That quantity is the total variation (TV) distance between the two distributions, which Divergences studies. It is 0 when the two distributions are equal, and 1 when they never produce the same outcome.
This limit splits security into three levels. If the TV distance is 0, the two worlds look identical and no adversary has any advantage, which is perfect security. If the TV distance is tiny, even an adversary with unlimited time gains almost nothing, which is statistical security. The third level is the main business of cryptography. There, the TV distance can be large, as long as no efficient adversary can find the outcomes where the two worlds differ. This is computational security. A short key cannot make the two worlds identical, but it can make their difference too hard to find, and that is how a short key protects a long message.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.3 Efficient adversaries and tiny advantages
No key resists every attacker. An attacker who tries keys one after another finds a 40-bit key quickly, and a 256-bit key never. Security is therefore a statement about how fast the attacker’s success shrinks as the key grows. Cryptographers measure the size of the key with a security parameter, written \(\lambda\), which you can think of as the key length in bits.
The asymptotic view describes what happens as \(\lambda\) grows, and it needs two definitions. The first says which attackers count as efficient. An attacker is efficient if its running time grows at most like a polynomial in \(\lambda\), such as the cube of \(\lambda\). Such an attacker may also flip coins as it runs. It is therefore called probabilistic polynomial time (PPT): probabilistic because of the coins, and polynomial time because of the bound on its running time.
The second definition says which advantages count as tiny. Think of the adversary’s advantage as a function of \(\lambda\). That function is negligible if it falls below one over every polynomial in \(\lambda\) once \(\lambda\) is large enough, and stays below it for all larger \(\lambda\). The function \(2^{-\lambda}\) is negligible, because \(2^\lambda\) outgrows every polynomial. The function \(\lambda^{-10}\) is not, because it never falls below \(\lambda^{-11}\). A scheme is secure if every PPT adversary has a negligible advantage.
The two definitions fit together for a reason. An efficient attacker can repeat its attack a polynomial number of times. The union bound from Concentration inequalities says that the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances. So the chance that at least one try succeeds is at most the number of tries times the chance per try. A negligible chance per try falls below one over any polynomial, including the number of tries times any other polynomial you pick. Multiplying it by the number of tries therefore still leaves it below one over that other polynomial, so repetition does not help.
A small chance that is not negligible does not survive repetition. Suppose an attack succeeds with probability \(\lambda^{-3}\) on each try, and the tries are independent. Independence lets the chances of failure multiply, so \(\lambda^4\) tries all fail with probability at most \(e^{-\lambda}\), and the attack almost surely succeeds.
Brute force shows why the best one can ask for is “negligible”, never zero. Suppose an attacker tries \(t\) different keys against a key drawn uniformly from all \(2^\lambda\) keys. Each try is right with probability \(2^{-\lambda}\), so the attacker succeeds with probability \(t/2^\lambda\). That chance is negligible when \(t\) is a polynomial in \(\lambda\), but it is never zero.
The weakness of these definitions is that “negligible” describes a limit, not a value at the key length you actually use. Table 8.1 evaluates four functions at \(\lambda = 128\). The negligible \(2^{-\sqrt\lambda}\) is still \(3.9\times10^{-4}\) there, far larger than the non-negligible \(\lambda^{-10}\). It drops below \(\lambda^{-10}\) for good only from \(\lambda = 20{,}520\) (Figure 8.1). A statement that holds “for all large enough \(\lambda\)” does not tell you whether 128 is large enough.

Real systems fix the key length. A block cipher encrypts data in blocks of fixed size under a key, and the standard one, AES, uses keys of 128 bits or more. Concrete security therefore replaces “efficient” and “negligible” by explicit numbers. It names the attacker’s resources and bounds the advantage they can buy. The resources are the attacker’s running time and the number of questions it may ask an oracle. An oracle is a box the game lets it query, such as one that encrypts messages of its choice. Brute force sets the benchmark. A scheme has \(\kappa\)-bit security if no attack does better than brute force over \(2^\kappa\) keys, where \(\kappa\) is a number of bits. In other words, an attacker that runs for time \(t\) gets an advantage of at most about \(t/2^\kappa\).
Here is what 128-bit security buys. Suppose an attacker tests \(10^{18}\) keys per second for a whole year, which is about \(2^{84.7}\) keys. Against a 128-bit key, the attack succeeds with probability \(9.3\times10^{-14}\). Trying all \(2^{128}\) keys would take \(1.08\times10^{13}\) years.
Security proofs are reductions. A scheme is built from a primitive, a simpler building block such as a block cipher. The reduction shows that an adversary who breaks the scheme can be turned into one that breaks the primitive. Read in reverse, if the primitive is hard to break, so is the scheme. The conversion usually loses something. Suppose a reduction turns an advantage against the scheme into one \(2^{20}\) times smaller against the primitive. If the primitive has 128-bit security, the scheme then has only about 108 bits. A tight reduction loses almost nothing, while a loose one forces larger keys for the same guarantee.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.4 Hybrid arguments
Proofs rarely compare the two worlds of a game directly. They walk from one to the other through intermediate worlds called hybrids, and each world differs from the next in one thing. Write \(m\) for the number of steps. Write \(H_i\) for the world reached after \(i\) steps. So \(H_0\) is the first world of the game and \(H_m\) is the second.
Look at how often a distinguisher says 1 in each world along the way. The gap between the two ends is the sum of the gaps between neighbours, since every intermediate frequency is added once and subtracted once. The size of a sum is at most the sum of the sizes, so the advantages add up: \[\mathrm{Adv}_A(H_0, H_m) \le \sum_{i=1}^m\mathrm{Adv}_A(H_{i-1}, H_i). \tag{8.3}\] Any gap between the two ends must show up in at least one step of the chain.
The most common use is for many samples. Suppose that one sample from \(X\) cannot be told from one sample from \(Y\). To compare \(m\) independent samples from each, walk from all samples drawn from \(X\) to all drawn from \(Y\), swapping one sample at a time. Each step changes a single sample, so it is a one-sample problem, and the total advantage is at most \(m\) times the one-sample advantage.
The argument needs two conditions. First, the number of samples \(m\) must be a polynomial in \(\lambda\). Otherwise \(m\) times a negligible advantage need not be negligible, and the bound says nothing. Second, both distributions must be efficiently samplable. The proof turns an attack on \(m\) samples into an attack on one sample. That attack places its one sample at a random position, and fills the other positions with samples it draws itself, from \(Y\) before that position and from \(X\) after it. If drawing samples were slow, the one-sample attack would no longer be efficient.
The factor \(m\) is safe but pessimistic, because it reflects how the proof is organized, not how the best attacker works. Take a coin that lands heads with probability 0.51, and compare \(m\) of its flips with \(m\) fair flips. Write \(\delta\) for the bias, here 0.01. One flip gives an advantage of at most \(\delta\), so the hybrid bound for \(m\) flips is \(m\delta\). Table 8.2 compares it with the best possible advantage and with a simple test, majority vote, which says 1 if more than half the flips are heads.

The hybrid bound is exact for one flip and useless by 100 flips. The best attacker counts the heads, and its advantage depends on how far apart the two average counts are compared with their random spread. The average counts differ by \(m\delta\), while each count spreads by about \(\sqrt m/2\) around its average. Their distance in units of the spread is therefore \(2\delta\sqrt m\), so the best advantage grows like \(\delta\sqrt m\), not like \(\delta m\) (Figure 8.2). To reach a constant advantage, such as one half, the attacker needs about \(1/\delta^2\) flips, while the hybrid bound would allow it after \(1/\delta\).






Figure 8.2: Advantage of telling \(m\) flips of a coin with bias \(\frac12 + 0.01\) from fair flips: majority vote (simulation), the best possible distinguisher (exact TV distance), and the hybrid bound \(m\delta\).



At 10,000 flips, majority vote reaches an advantage of only 0.481. The best possible is 0.683. Its threshold of half the flips sits at the centre of the fair coin’s count. For many flips, the biased count lands above that threshold almost always, but the fair count still lands above it about half the time. So the advantage of majority vote can never exceed about one half. The best test puts its threshold halfway between the two average counts instead. A reasonable-looking test can thus be far from the best one, which is why security is measured against every adversary.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.5 Pseudorandom generators and functions
Truly random bits are expensive to produce and to share, while a short random key is cheap. Two tools stretch a short key into a lot of randomness that looks real to any efficient observer.
A pseudorandom generator (PRG) is a fast, deterministic procedure that stretches a short random seed into a longer string. It is secure if no efficient distinguisher can tell its output from truly random bits of the same length.
A PRG can never be statistically secure. Suppose its output is at least one bit longer than its seed. Then there are at most half as many seeds as output strings, so at most half of all strings of that length are outputs of the PRG. A distinguisher that says 1 exactly on those outputs always says 1 on the PRG’s output, and at most half the time on random bits. Its advantage is therefore at least one half. But checking whether a string is an output means trying every seed, which takes exponential time. Pseudorandomness is therefore only a promise against efficient distinguishers.
PRGs exist if one-way functions exist, which are functions that are easy to compute but hard to invert. A stream cipher, such as ChaCha20, encrypts by combining the data with a long keystream generated from a short key. Designers treat stream ciphers as PRGs, which means assuming that no efficient distinguisher can tell the keystream from random bits.
A random function is a table that gives each input its own independent, uniform output. A table on 128-bit inputs has \(2^{128}\) entries, so nobody can store one.
A pseudorandom function (PRF) is a keyed function, written \(F_k\) for the key \(k\), whose outputs look like those of a random function to anyone without the key. Its game uses an oracle. A fair coin decides whether the box holds \(F_k\) with a freshly drawn random key, or a truly random function. The adversary may ask the box for its output on any inputs it likes, each one chosen after seeing the earlier answers. The PRF is secure if no efficient adversary can tell which function is in the box. In practice, the hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) is assumed to be a PRF.
A PRF can be built from any PRG whose output is twice as long as its seed. The construction is called the GGM tree, after Goldreich, Goldwasser and Micali. It grows a binary tree of keys, with the secret key at the root. The PRG applied to a node gives two halves, which become its two children. Each bit of the input picks the left or the right child, and the leaf reached at the end is the output.
The proof of the GGM tree is a chain of hybrids that replaces the tree by random values, one level at a time. Write \(n\) for the number of input bits, which is also the number of levels, and \(q\) for the number of queries the adversary makes. At each level the \(q\) queries touch at most \(q\) nodes, so each step of the chain costs at most \(q\) times the PRG’s advantage. Over the \(n\) levels, any efficient adversary’s advantage against the PRF is at most \(nq\) times the PRG’s advantage. The full edition sketches this proof and cites the complete one.
In proofs, both tools play the same role. They let you replace “pseudorandom” by “truly random”, at the cost of a small advantage.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.6 The birthday bound
Many arguments about random values fail only if two of the values happen to coincide. The birthday bound says how likely that is. Draw \(q\) values independently and uniformly from a set of size \(N\). The values form about \(q^2/2\) pairs. Each pair coincides with probability \(1/N\), because whatever the first value is, the second matches it with probability \(1/N\). So collisions become likely once the number of pairs approaches \(N\). That happens after about \(\sqrt N\) draws, far fewer than \(N\). Precisely, \[1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)} \le \Pr[\text{collision}] \le \frac{q(q-1)}{2N}. \tag{8.4}\]
The upper bound is the union bound over all pairs. The lower bound comes from the exact chance of no collision, which multiplies the chances that each new value misses all earlier ones. The two bounds are close. The full edition shows that, while the upper bound is below 1, it overstates the true chance by a factor of at most about 1.6. It also computes that a collision becomes as likely as not at about \(1.18\sqrt N\) draws.
The bound needs the values to be uniform and independent, because that is what makes each pair coincide with probability \(1/N\). Values that are not uniform coincide more often, so the upper bound can then fail.

Random 32-bit identifiers for 100,000 records clash more often than not. There, the union bound is above 1 and says nothing, while the lower bound is accurate. The birthday bound also limits how much data one key may protect, and the reason runs through block ciphers. A block cipher is a keyed permutation, which never maps two different inputs to the same output. It is modelled as a pseudorandom permutation (PRP), a keyed function that no efficient adversary can tell from a random shuffle of the inputs. Many proofs, such as the encryption proof in the next section, are written for a PRF instead, whose outputs on different inputs are independent. A permutation’s outputs are not quite independent, since they can never repeat.
The only visible difference between a random function and a random permutation is that the function sometimes repeats an output and the permutation never does. So an adversary can tell them apart only about as often as the answers collide. This is the switching lemma. Write \(n\) for the number of bits in a block, so that there are \(2^n\) possible blocks. Treating a PRP as a PRF then costs an extra advantage, on top of its advantage as a PRP. After \(q\) queries, the lemma bounds that extra advantage by \(q^2/2^{n+1}\), the birthday bound for \(2^n\) values. The bound is tight, because an adversary that says 1 when it sees a repeated answer has an advantage equal to the exact chance of a collision.
So a bound in terms of queries is really a limit on data. Take blocks of 128 bits, so that \(2^{32}\) blocks hold 64 GiB of data. That much data costs an extra advantage of at most \(2^{-65}\). At \(2^{48}\) blocks the bound has grown to \(2^{-33}\), and at \(2^{64}\) blocks it reaches one half and says nothing. The guarantee degrades with the square of the data under one key, which is why you should change keys long before that point. Ciphers with 64-bit blocks fare much worse. To keep the extra advantage below \(2^{-20}\), they can process only about 6 million blocks under one key.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.7 Encryption
An encryption scheme has perfect secrecy if the ciphertext’s distribution is the same for every message. Seeing the ciphertext then does not change how likely any message is.
The one-time pad achieves this. Its key \(K\) is a uniformly random string as long as the message \(m\). The ciphertext is \(m \oplus K\), where \(\oplus\) is the bitwise exclusive or (XOR), which flips each bit of the message where the key has a 1. For a fixed message, each key gives a different ciphertext, and each ciphertext comes from exactly one key. A uniform key therefore gives a uniform ciphertext, whatever the message is. Table 8.4 shows this for 2-bit messages.



Table 8.4: The one-time pad on 2-bit messages. Each row contains every ciphertext once, so the ciphertext is uniform for every message.

Perfect secrecy has a price, because it needs at least as many keys as messages. Fix a ciphertext that occurs. Because decryption must recover the message, each key decrypts it to one message, so it can come from at most as many messages as there are keys. With fewer keys than messages, some message could never produce that ciphertext, and seeing it would rule that message out. The pad must also be used only once. Combining two ciphertexts under the same pad with XOR cancels the pad and reveals the XOR of the two messages.
Practical schemes use short keys, so they settle for computational security. The standard goal is security under chosen-plaintext attack (CPA), defined by a game. The adversary may ask an oracle for encryptions of any messages it likes, at any time. It then submits two messages of equal length and receives the encryption of one of them, chosen by a fair coin. It must guess which one it got. The equal length is required because a ciphertext usually reveals the length of its message. The encryption oracle models reality, since an attacker can often get chosen data encrypted, such as a request it sends or a value it plants in a database. Passing this game is equivalent to a scheme hiding everything an efficient adversary could compute about the message, apart from its length.
The game has a consequence that surprises many programmers, which is that encryption must be randomized. Suppose encrypting the same message always gives the same ciphertext. The adversary asks for the encryption of its first message, then compares it with the challenge. Two different messages never share a ciphertext, because decryption could not then tell which one to return. So if the two ciphertexts match, the adversary got the first message, and otherwise the second. It is always right, so its advantage is 1, and the full edition’s script measures exactly 1.000.
The same weakness shows up without any game. Deterministic encryption of a column of labels maps equal labels to equal ciphertexts, so the frequency of each ciphertext reveals the frequency of each label.
The fix is to use a fresh pad for every encryption. Draw a random value \(r\), called a nonce, uniformly from a set of possible values, written \(\mathcal R\). Use \(F_k(r)\), the PRF’s output on \(r\), as a one-time pad, and send \(r\) along so that the receiver can rebuild the pad. The ciphertext is the pair \((r, m \oplus F_k(r))\).
This scheme can fail in only two ways. Either the PRF can be told from a random function, or the challenge reuses a nonce that the adversary has already seen. A reused nonce is fatal because the adversary knows its pad. Each encryption it requested showed it a nonce together with the ciphertext of a message it chose, and combining the two with XOR reveals the pad for that nonce. If the challenge reuses that nonce, the adversary removes the pad and reads the message.
The bound adds the two failures. Write \(q\) for the number of encryptions the adversary requests, and \(\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\) for the number of possible nonces. By the union bound, the challenge’s nonce matches one of the \(q\) earlier ones with probability at most \(q/\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\). The advantage is then at most twice the PRF’s advantage plus \(q/\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\). The factor 2 comes from converting a win probability into an advantage, by the rule in Section 8.2.
The second term is real, not a weakness of the proof. Take 8-bit nonces and 16 encryptions. An attacker who waits for a repeated nonce then wins with advantage 0.0607, against a bound of 0.0625. The simulation measures 0.0605. With 128-bit nonces, the same attack has an advantage below \(2^{-124}\).
The proof needs only the challenge’s nonce to differ from the earlier ones, and that costs at most \(q/\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\), which grows in proportion to \(q\). Over the life of a key, though, any two nonces may repeat, and each repeat reuses a pad. By the birthday bound, repeats become likely after about \(\sqrt{\lvert\mathcal R\rvert}\) encryptions, so size the nonce set for that.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.8 Simulation and secret sharing
Encryption hides everything. Many procedures instead run among several participants, each holding its own input, and must reveal something to each of them, such as the final result, and nothing else. “Nothing else” is hard to state directly, because a participant may combine what it sees in clever ways. Simulation sidesteps the problem. Suppose a participant could have faked everything it sees from what it is allowed to learn. Then what it sees contains nothing more.
A participant’s view, written \(\mathrm{View}(x)\), is everything it sees during a run, which depends on all the inputs \(x\) and on the procedure’s randomness. Write \(L(x)\) for what it is allowed to learn, such as its own input and the output. A simulator, written \(S\), is an efficient procedure that receives only \(L(x)\) and produces a fake view. The procedure reveals nothing beyond \(L(x)\) if the fake view has the same distribution as the real one, for every input \(x\): \[S(L(x)) \equiv \mathrm{View}(x). \tag{8.5}\] This is perfect security. If the two distributions are only close in TV distance, the security is statistical. If no efficient distinguisher can tell them apart, it is computational.
The definition captures “nothing else” for a simple reason. Anything the participant could compute from its real view, it could compute equally well from the simulator’s output. That output was made from \(L(x)\) alone, so whatever the view reveals, \(L(x)\) already revealed. The simulator must be efficient. In computational security, an unbounded simulator could compute things the participant cannot. The definition would then accept views that reveal facts that are easy to read from the view but hard to compute from \(L(x)\). Finally, the definition compares the view only with \(L(x)\), so it says nothing about whether revealing \(L(x)\) itself is acceptable. That is decided when you choose \(L\).
Additive secret sharing is the simplest example. It works with the integers from 0 to \(p - 1\), where \(p\) is the modulus and arithmetic wraps around mod \(p\). To split a secret \(x\) among \(h\) holders, draw \(h - 1\) shares independently and uniformly at random. Set the last share to \(x\) minus the sum of the others, mod \(p\). All the shares then add up to \(x\). Suppose two secrets are shared among the same holders, and each holder adds its share of one to its share of the other. The results are shares of the sum of the secrets, so the holders can compute a sum without ever putting their shares together.
Any \(h - 1\) of the shares look like independent uniform numbers, whatever the secret is, because the one missing share is what ties them to \(x\). The reason is that subtracting a uniform number mod \(p\) wraps around and hits every value equally often. Table 8.5 shows this for two holders and \(p = 5\). As the random first share \(r\) runs through all five values, the second share \(x - r\) takes each value exactly once, for either secret. The simulator for a group of \(h - 1\) holders therefore just outputs uniform random numbers. The fake view has exactly the real distribution, so the security is perfect.

Suppose the group of \(h - 1\) holders also learns the secret, for example because it is published later. The simulator then receives \(x\). It draws the group’s \(h - 1\) shares uniformly, and these shares together with \(x\) fix the one missing share as \(x\) minus their sum. This matches the real shares exactly. It is the typical form of a simulator, random where the view is random and consistent with the leakage where the leakage pins the view down.
The wrap-around is a condition of the result, not a detail. Without it, the share’s range moves with the secret. Suppose the mask \(r\) is uniform on the 16 values from 0 to 15, and the share \(x - r\) is not reduced. Call the number of possible masks, here 16, the mask width \(W\). The share then lies in a window of 16 values that ends at the secret itself. The window for the secret 7 starts seven places above the window for the secret 0. Seven of the 16 values in each window are impossible under the other secret, so the TV distance is \(7/16 = 0.4375\). A simulation with 100,000 shares for each secret measures 0.4423 (Figure 8.4).
For comparison, the simulation also draws \(r\) uniformly from 0 to 10 and reduces the share \(x - r\) modulo 11. The measured TV distance is then 0.0045, which is sampling noise, since the exact distance is zero. In general, without the wrap-around, the TV distance is the difference between the two secrets divided by the mask width \(W\), as long as that difference is smaller than \(W\). A much wider mask makes it tiny, which gives statistical rather than perfect security.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.9 Learning with errors
Every tool so far is defined by a property, such as looking random, and works with any primitive that has it. Learning with errors (LWE) is instead a specific hard problem, with three attractions. Under a condition on its errors, it is as hard as worst-case problems on lattices, regular grids of points in many dimensions. No efficient quantum attack on it is known. And encryption built on it lets you add ciphertexts without decrypting them.
LWE hides a secret vector behind linear equations whose right-hand sides are slightly wrong. The secret \(s\) is a vector of numbers mod \(p\), and its length \(d\) is called the dimension. Each sample pairs a uniformly random vector \(a\) with a number \(b\).
To compute that number, take the inner product \(\langle a, s\rangle\), the sum of the products of matching entries. Then add the error \(e\), a small random integer drawn fresh for each sample, and reduce mod \(p\). The search version of the problem asks for \(s\). The decision version asks whether a list of pairs consists of LWE samples or of uniform random pairs.
The errors are what make the problem hard. Without them, the samples form a linear system, and Gaussian elimination solves it from \(d\) independent equations. With them, elimination solves the wrong system exactly. Undoing the equations multiplies the small errors by large numbers mod \(p\), which scrambles the answer. The full edition’s script shows this with a 16-dimensional secret and \(p = 4096\). Without errors, elimination recovers all 16 coordinates. With small errors of \(-1\), 0 or 1, it recovers none of them.
Hardness holds under a condition on the errors. Regev proved it for errors drawn from a normal distribution rounded to integers, with a standard deviation large enough relative to \(\sqrt d\). Under that condition, solving LWE is at least as hard as worst-case lattice problems. His proof used a quantum algorithm, and later work gave classical proofs. Other small error distributions, such as the uniform errors in the toy below, need separate arguments. The full edition cites these results rather than proving them.
Regev encryption of a single bit uses LWE directly. It is a secret-key scheme, in which the same secret \(s\) encrypts and decrypts. Picture the numbers mod \(p\) as a clock with \(p\) positions, where \(p\) is even. To encrypt a bit \(m\), take a fresh LWE sample and move its \(b\) halfway round the clock if the bit is 1. Whoever knows \(s\) subtracts \(\langle a, s\rangle\). What remains is the error plus the encoded bit, which is near 0 for the bit 0 and near halfway for the bit 1. Decryption reads off whichever is closer. It is correct as long as the error is smaller than a quarter of the clock, \(\lvert e\rvert < p/4\). A larger error could push the value past the boundary between the two halves.
Without the key, the sample looks uniform, by the decision version of LWE. The bit is then added to something that looks uniform, which works like a one-time pad. That is why the scheme is secure against chosen-plaintext attack, provided that decision LWE is hard.
Adding ciphertexts entry by entry adds everything inside them. The bits add, and two half-turns round the clock make a full turn, so the sum decrypts to the XOR of the bits. Two half-turns make exactly a full turn only when \(p\) is even, which is why the scheme needs an even \(p\). The errors add as well. Suppose every error lies between \(-B\) and \(B\), where \(B\) is the error bound. A sum of \(k\) ciphertexts then has an error of at most \(kB\), and it decrypts correctly whenever \[k < \frac{p}{4B}. \tag{8.6}\] With \(p = 4096\) and \(B = 32\), the budget guarantees that sums of fewer than 32 ciphertexts decrypt correctly.
That guarantee is a worst case. It assumes every error is as large as possible and all have the same sign. Independent errors with mean zero mostly cancel instead. Their variances add, so the summed error has a standard deviation that grows like \(\sqrt k\), not like \(k\). Table 8.6 compares a simulation with a normal approximation built on this fact.

Take a sum of 1,024 ciphertexts as an example. The full edition computes the standard deviation of the summed error from the variance of the individual errors. It gets about 600. A quarter of the clock is 1,024, about 1.7 standard deviations. A normal value lands that far from zero with probability about 0.088. Failures become measurable only for sums of around 256 ciphertexts, eight times the guaranteed 32 (Figure 8.5).






Figure 8.5: Decryption failure rate of a sum of \(k\) Regev ciphertexts (\(p = 4096\), errors uniform on \(\{-32, \dots, 32\}\)): simulation against the normal approximation. The dashed line is the worst-case guarantee \(k < p/(4B) = 32\).



But the budget is still finite. Once the error is comparable to a quarter of the clock, the decrypted value is spread round the whole clock, and decryption becomes a coin flip. A larger modulus, relative to the error, buys more additions. That trade-off sets the parameters of every LWE-based scheme that computes on ciphertexts.
A Regev ciphertext carries one bit in \(d + 1\) numbers, which is wasteful. Practical lattice schemes use structured variants of LWE, such as ring-LWE and module-LWE, which pack many values into each ciphertext and compute faster. Module-LWE underlies ML-KEM, the standardized scheme for sending a fresh shared key, published as FIPS 203 in 2024.

Eventually below one over every polynomial in \(\lambda\); survives polynomially many repetitions


\(\kappa\)-bit security
Time \(t\) buys an advantage of at most about \(t/2^\kappa\)


Hybrid argument
Advantages add along a chain; \(m\) samples cost at most a factor \(m\)


Birthday bound
\(1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)} \le \Pr[\text{collision}] \le q(q-1)/(2N)\); 50% at \(q \approx 1.18\sqrt N\)


PRP to PRF switching
Extra advantage at most \(q^2/2^{n+1}\) for \(n\)-bit blocks, and tight


GGM tree
PRF advantage at most \(nq\) times the PRG advantage


One-time pad
Perfect secrecy; needs as many keys as messages; never reuse the pad


CPA security
Deterministic schemes have advantage 1; \((r, m \oplus F_k(r))\) has advantage at most \(2\,\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} + q/\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\)


Simulation
Secure if a simulator fakes the view from the allowed leakage \(L(x)\)


Additive sharing mod \(p\)
Any \(h - 1\) shares are uniform: perfect security


Regev encryption
Correct if \(\lvert e\rvert < p/4\); sums of \(k\) ciphertexts correct if \(kB < p/4\); typical error grows like \(\sqrt k\)






Rules of thumb

Security of \(\kappa\) bits means an attacker with time \(t\) succeeds with probability about \(t/2^\kappa\).
Random values of \(\kappa\) bits collide after about \(2^{\kappa/2}\) draws. Size identifiers, nonces and key lifetimes accordingly.
Encryption that hides whether two messages are equal must be randomized.
In LWE schemes, the error is a budget that each operation spends.

text:

It cites the existence of PRGs, the hardness of LWE, and the equivalence between passing the CPA game and hiding everything an efficient adversary could compute. It also only sketches the proof for the GGM tree.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
The common thread
This part teaches you to break models before the rest of the book teaches you to protect them, and the order is deliberate. A privacy defence is a promise that some adversary cannot learn some secret, and you cannot judge the promise until you know who the adversary is, what it sees and how well the best one could do. An evaluation that calls a model private is likewise only as honest as the attack it ran.
Read this part if you have to decide whether a trained model, a released dataset or a set of published statistics leaks information about the people behind it, whether you build the system, audit it or review a report about it. You need the true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) of a test from the Prerequisites; each chapter restates what it uses. Differential privacy (DP), the defence most of the book is about, comes in the next part, and it is built to defeat exactly the games set up here.
Every attack in this part is a game. A challenger trains a model or releases statistics that depend on a hidden secret, the adversary gets the view its threat model allows, and it guesses the secret. Only the secret changes from chapter to chapter: whether a record was used, a sensitive field, a memorized string, a name, the whole dataset. Writing attacks this way forces two questions that reports often leave open: what was the adversary assumed to see and know, and how well would a guess have done without the view?
When the secret is one bit, the game is a hypothesis test. The adversary sees one output and must decide which world produced it, the one with the record or the one without. The best it can do is ask how much more likely that output is in one world than in the other, and accuse where that ratio is largest. This best test depends only on the two distributions of what the adversary sees, so its success caps every attack, including those not yet invented. The strongest practical membership attack, the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA), approximates it, which is why it is the one to run in an audit.
The second idea is that the worst case is not the average case. A model leaks most about the records it cannot predict without having seen them: outliers, duplicated strings, unique combinations of attributes. An average over all records dilutes those few into a harmless-looking number. Yet a verdict like “this person was in the data” only harms someone when it is confident, which requires that the attack almost never accuses the wrong person. So attacks are scored by their TPR at a low FPR, and a defence has to hold for every record.
A third idea closes the part: answer enough statistics accurately enough and the answers pin the data down, however they were computed. Some noise is not optional, and the next part asks how little is enough.

title: Threat models and attacks
section: Why the chapters come in this order
text:
Why the chapters come in this order
Threat models and privacy games comes first because it fixes the vocabulary the others use: view, game, advantage, baseline, and the ceiling on any attack. Membership inference follows because its secret is the smallest, one bit, and the attacks on models after it build on it; it is also the attack you will run most often. The next four chapters attack models for larger secrets, in any order: a sensitive field in Attribute inference and model inversion, a fact about the training population in Property inference, training text in Memorization and training-data extraction, and the input behind a gradient in Gradient inversion.
The last three chapters attack released data, from the weakest defence to the strongest. Linkage and re-identification shows that removing names fails when a few attributes single a person out. Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks hides each record in a crowd of look-alikes and shows the attacks that get past it. Reconstruction attacks releases only aggregates and shows that enough accurate ones give the data back. Read these in order: each releases less than the one before, and each still leaks.
Each chapter opens with the practical question and the idea that answers it, explains each result with its reason, and ends with a cheat sheet. The examples are toys whose numbers come from the full edition’s scripts, which also hold the derivations.

title: Threat models and attacks
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
You will be able to state any attack as a game with a threat model and a baseline, and refuse to read its number until you know both. You will run a membership audit with shadow models and LiRA, report it as a TPR at a low FPR with the number of non-members behind it, and explain why the exposed records are the outliers. You will tell a leak about individuals from inference about the population, and know why rounding confidences does not close it. And you will know why removing names, hiding records in crowds and publishing only aggregates each fail, which is the case for the guarantee of the next part.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model on patient records and offers it to doctors through a web service. Is the model private? The question has no answer until you say against whom. An attacker who reads only predicted labels sees far less than one who downloads the weights, and one who knows every other patient in the training set can isolate a single record far better than one who knows only the population. A threat model fixes these assumptions. Without one, “the model leaks” and “the model is safe” are both untestable, and two attack numbers cannot be compared.
Once the threat model is fixed, an attack becomes a game. A challenger runs the pipeline with a hidden secret, such as whether one patient’s record was used, hands the adversary what the threat model lets it see, its view, and the adversary guesses the secret. The one idea of this chapter: an attack is worth only its margin over a guess made without the view. When the secret is one bit, the game is a hypothesis test: the best attack can be worked out and caps every real one, and what matters is how it does when it almost never accuses the wrong person.
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.2 Threat models
A threat model answers five questions.

Goal: the secret. Membership of a record, a sensitive field of a known record (attribute), the records themselves (reconstruction), or a statistic of the whole dataset (property).
Access: from least to most, the model’s decisions on chosen inputs (label-only), its scores such as confidences or losses (black-box), its parameters (white-box), or everything training exposed, such as per-step gradients (the transcript).
Behaviour: an honest-but-curious adversary only analyses what it legitimately sees; a malicious one may query adaptively, insert crafted records into the training data (poisoning) or tamper with the protocol.
Trust: a trusted curator holds the data (central model), or nobody is trusted (local model).
Side information: the population, a public dataset, some or all of the other records, the target’s non-sensitive fields.

Access is the one axis with a natural order, because each level lets the adversary compute the level below: from the weights it can compute any score, from a score the label, and the final weights are the last entry of the transcript. Whatever an attack does with less access, an adversary with more access can do too, by first throwing the extra away. So for the best attack at each level, \[\text{best advantage from labels} \le \text{from scores} \le \text{from weights} \le \text{from the transcript}, \tag{9.1}\] and likewise for the best true positive rate (TPR) at every false positive rate (FPR), defined in Section 9.3. More side information or permission to cheat never weakens the best adversary either, since it can ignore what it knows and choose to behave. The same reasoning tells you what output tweaks do: noising or rounding returned scores, or returning labels only, is processing the adversary could have done itself, so it can lower the best attack but never raise it.
A service returning the top class gives label-only access, one returning confidences black-box access, published weights white-box access, and a federated-training server sees the transcript; a model exposed in several ways is as risky as the most exposed. Side information is the axis you control least, so a guarantee should survive the strongest assumption: an adversary who knows every record except the target’s, which a malicious one approaches by planting records.
The chain compares the best attacks, not the ones people run. A security team fits the simplest anomaly detector: the mean \(\theta\) of \(n = 100\) records with \(d = 50\) normal features, flagging a point \(x\) when its score \(\|x - \theta\|^2\) exceeds \(\tau = d\). Training on a record pulls \(\theta\) slightly towards it, so a member sits a little closer to \(\theta\) than it otherwise would. But some targets are far from the mean whether or not they were used, so the raw score mixes “unusual record” with “not a member”. The calibrated score \(\|z\|^2 - \|z - \theta\|^2\) subtracts the target’s own distance from the origin and leaves how far \(\theta\) leans towards \(z\). That is almost exactly the white-box likelihood ratio: it drops only a term that shifts the threshold from one target to the next, and in this model the score carries everything about \(\theta\) the decision needs.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.3 Privacy games and baselines
A game pins down how the secret and data are drawn, what the adversary sees, and how its guess is scored against a baseline, the best guess from the side information alone. The baseline is part of the game: a model that lets an attacker guess a rare diagnosis “with 90% accuracy” reveals nothing if 90% of people do not have it.
In the membership game a hidden bit \(b\) decides the world: \(b = 1\) means the target’s record is in the training set (it is a member), \(b = 0\) that it is a fresh draw from the population. The attack’s true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members it flags, its false positive rate (FPR) the fraction of non-members it wrongly flags. With prior \(\pi_1\) that \(b = 1\) and \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi_1\), it wins with probability \(\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\), since the prior decides how many games are played in each world. That is the trap. An attack with TPR 0.6 and FPR 0.2 wins 0.7 of games at a fair prior and 0.78 at \(\pi_1 = 0.1\), which looks better but is worse: always saying “not a member” wins 0.9 there.
The fix is to score the attack inside each world. The advantage \[\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \tag{9.2}\] is how much more often the attack says “member” to members than to non-members. An attack that ignores its view says “member” equally often in both worlds and scores 0 at any prior; a perfect attack scores 1; and at a fair prior the winning probability is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\). The attack above has advantage 0.4 whatever the prior.
When the bit is rare, the best attack keeps the default guess “0” and overturns it on a view only when that gains more than it costs. Saying “1” on a view wins the games where \(b = 1\), in proportion to \(\pi_1\) times the view’s probability in that world, and loses those where \(b = 0\), in proportion to \(\pi_0\) times its probability there. So it says “1” only on views more than \(\pi_0/\pi_1\) times as likely when the bit is 1: 9 times at \(\pi_1 = 0.1\). Take a count of people with a sensitive condition, published with unit Gaussian noise, and an adversary who knows every other record. At a fair prior the best guess of the target’s bit is right with probability 0.6915. At prior 0.1 the baseline is 0.9 and the best guess reaches only 0.9013: one record shifts the count by one standard deviation of noise, which rarely yields 9-to-1 evidence.
The other games change the secret and the baseline. In the attribute game the secret is a sensitive field of a known member, and comparing with a guess from the population asks only “does the model help?”. Comparing the attack’s success on members with its success on non-members asks “does it help because this person was in the data?”, and only that is a breach of the person’s privacy (Attribute inference and model inversion). The reconstruction and property games target the records and a statistic of the population; like membership, they draw data from the population and so measure an average case. The distinguishing game lets the adversary choose two datasets that differ in one record, a worst case (Section 9.5).
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.4 Advantage, total variation and TPR at a low FPR
text:
9.4 Advantage, total variation and TPR at a low FPR
A two-world game is a test of “not a member” against “member”, so the results of Hypothesis testing become ceilings on every attack. Write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the distributions of the adversary’s view without and with the target. Flagging a set of views costs its probability under \(P\) in false positives and earns its probability under \(Q\) in true positives, so with a fixed budget of false positives the best attack flags the views with the largest likelihood ratio \(q/p\) first. That gives two ceilings: \[\mathrm{Adv} \le \mathrm{TV}(P, Q), \qquad \mathrm{TPR} \le 1 - T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.3}\] The total variation (TV) distance is the advantage of flagging exactly the views more likely under \(Q\). The trade-off function \(T(P, Q)(\alpha)\) is the smallest fraction of members any attack with FPR \(\alpha\) must miss. The first ceiling caps one point of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, the plot of TPR against FPR as the threshold moves; the second caps the whole curve. Both depend only on \(P\) and \(Q\), so they bound attacks nobody has invented yet, which makes them the right target for a defence.
But the advantage is the wrong point of the curve to report. It is where TPR − FPR is largest, while privacy breaks at the end where the attack almost never accuses a non-member. An attack that flags 1% of members with no false alarms has advantage about 0.01, yet identifies them with certainty; one right on 55% of members and wrong on 45% of non-members has advantage 0.1 and identifies nobody with confidence. What a flagged person cares about is the precision, the share of “member” verdicts that are right: a fraction \(\pi_1\) of targets are members and the attack flags TPR of them, a fraction \(\pi_0\) are not and it flags FPR of those, so \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flagged}] = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{9.4}\] Only a small FPR keeps this high, and the rarer members are, the smaller it must be.
The noisy count with the other 100 records known shows the trade. The best attack says “member” where the two bell curves cross, with advantage \(\mathrm{TV} = 0.3829\) (0.3809 over 200,000 simulated games per world). Hold the FPR at \(10^{-3}\) instead: the threshold rises until one non-member in a thousand passes, and the TPR falls to 0.0183. The attack catches fewer than 2% of members, but when it fires it is right with precision 0.948 at a fair prior, or 0.156 if one target in a hundred is a member. So report the TPR at a low FPR such as \(10^{-3}\), draw the ROC curve on log axes where that end is visible (Figure 9.2), and state the prior with any precision.






Figure 9.2: Left: the released count in the two worlds when the other 100 records are known (solid) and unknown (dashed). Right: the membership ROC curves of the best attacks on log axes. The dotted diagonal is random guessing.
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.5 Average case and worst case
An average-case game draws the data and the target from the population, and the adversary knows only the population. A worst-case game lets the adversary know, or choose, the other records and the target. The noisy count shows why they differ. An adversary who does not know the other 100 records sees an average over all the crowds they might form, and the target’s single unit of shift is buried under their uncertainty, which acts like extra noise of variance 25 on top of the released noise of variance 1. Knowing the crowd removes that blur, and choosing it picks the crowd where the target stands out most. So the best advantage only grows from not knowing, to knowing, to choosing (Table 9.2).

Not knowing the crowd cuts the advantage by a factor of five, and turns an exact count from a complete giveaway into a small leak; as the crowd grows the average case falls further while the worst case does not move (Figure 9.3). A defence that relies on that blur fails against an adversary who knows the other records or planted them.






Figure 9.3: Best membership advantage on the noisy count against the number \(m\) of other records the adversary does not know, for three noise levels (solid), and against an adversary who knows them (dashed). The average case falls as the crowd grows; the worst case does not move.



Averaging over targets hides people in the same way. A mechanism that publishes one record chosen at random among \(n = 1000\) has an average advantage of \(1/n = 0.001\) and looks almost perfectly safe, yet every run exposes one person completely. Privacy is a promise to each person, so what matters is the advantage against the worst-off one.
Average-case numbers, which are what an audit can estimate, are therefore lower bounds on the worst case, never upper bounds. Audits narrow the gap by playing the adversary who chooses the target: they plant canaries, records built to be as exposed as possible, and attack those (Memorization and training-data extraction). The guarantee of The definition of differential privacy goes all the way: it bounds the worst case for every pair of datasets that differ in one record, and so every membership-style game at once.
