title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.6 Code
When the attack score is a unit normal for non-members and shifted for members, the best TPR at any FPR and the precision take a few lines:
from statistics import NormalDist

Z = NormalDist()


def tpr_at_fpr(fpr: float, shift: float) -> float:
    """Best TPR at a given FPR when the attack score is N(0, 1) for non-members, N(shift, 1) for members."""
    return 1 - Z.cdf(Z.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - shift)


def precision(tpr: float, fpr: float, prior: float) -> float:
    """Fraction of 'member' verdicts that are right when a fraction `prior` of targets are members."""
    return prior * tpr / (prior * tpr + (1 - prior) * fpr)


advantage = 2 * Z.cdf(0.5) - 1  # best TPR - FPR for a shift of 1: the total variation distance
tpr = tpr_at_fpr(1e-3, 1.0)
print(f"{advantage:.4f}")  # 0.3829
print(f"{tpr:.4f}")  # 0.0183
print(f"{precision(tpr, 1e-3, 0.5):.3f}")  # 0.948
print(f"{precision(tpr, 1e-3, 0.01):.3f}")  # 0.156
The full edition’s script, threat_models.py, computes every number in this chapter and checks it by simulation:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/threat_models.py

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model to predict a disease and publishes it. You hold one patient’s record. Was that record in the training set? If it was, you have learned that the patient was treated there for that disease. This is membership inference, the standard way to measure leakage: if an attacker cannot even tell whether a record was used, it can do little else with it. An attack is scored by its true positive rate (TPR), the fraction of members it flags, and its false positive rate (FPR), the fraction of non-members it wrongly flags; its advantage is TPR minus FPR (Threat models and privacy games).
The one idea: membership inference is a test about one record. Train a model many times on data containing a target record and look at its output on that record; train it without the record and look again. Training is random, so each case gives a distribution, the record’s IN and OUT distributions, and the attacker must say which one an output came from. A typical record is predicted well whether or not the model saw it, so its two distributions nearly coincide; an atypical record is predicted badly unless the model saw it, so they are far apart. So one threshold for every record confuses “easy record” with “member”, strong attacks compare each record with itself, and the exposed records are the atypical ones.
The numbers come from one experiment, the setup of Carlini et al. (2022) scaled down to a linear model: a pool of 950 typical points and 50 outliers whose label is a coin flip, so a model gets an outlier right only by fitting it; regularized logistic regression trained on random halves of the pool, 128 target and 64 shadow models; 64,000 member and 64,000 non-member pairs.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.2 The loss attack and the generalization gap
text:
10.2 The loss attack and the generalization gap
A model fits its training data better than other data, so the simplest attack, due to Yeom et al. (2018), says “member” when the loss is low. Its advantage is a number you already know. Let the loss \(\ell\) lie in \([0, B]\) and say “member” with probability \(1 - \ell/B\). Then the TPR is one minus the average member loss over \(B\), the FPR the same with the non-member loss, and their difference is the gap between the two average losses, which are the training and test loss: \[\mathrm{Adv} = \frac{\text{expected test loss} - \text{expected training loss}}{B}. \tag{10.1}\] With the 0-1 loss the attack is “member if classified correctly”, with advantage test error minus training error.
In the running example the training error is 0.1495 and the test error 0.2663, and “member if correctly classified” has TPR 0.8505, FPR 0.7337 and advantage 0.1168, exactly the gap. Yet it identifies nobody with confidence, flagging almost three non-members in four (Figure 10.1).






Figure 10.1: Distribution of \(\phi\), the logit of the target model’s confidence in the true label, over member and non-member pairs. The dashed line is the mean-training-loss threshold: the attack says “member” to its right.



So overfitting implies leakage, and you can read a lower bound off train and test error without running anything. The converse fails because of what the gap averages: it equals the average self-influence of the training records, how much each record’s own loss rises when it is left out. An average hides who is memorized, and an attack that ignores which record it is looking at cannot find them. A small gap does not mean a private model.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.3 Shadow models
A better attack needs to know what members’ outputs look like, without seeing the target’s training set. Shokri et al. (2017) had the attacker train shadow models of its own, with the same recipe on data from the same population, so that it knows who was a member of each. It labels their outputs “in” and “out” and trains an attack model to classify them. With enough shadow data the attack model learns the probability of membership given the output, which is the best test that output allows. But the output is pooled over records, so this is the best attack among those that treat all records alike: it cannot know that a given confidence is high for one record and low for another. Here it amounts to a per-class loss threshold.
What shadow models really buy is calibration: the attacker sets its threshold where a chosen fraction of its own shadow non-members pass, and trusts the real non-members to behave the same. Set for an FPR of 1% on the shadows, the threshold gives 0.0095 on the target models, but its TPR there is 0.0098, chance. Imitate the target’s recipe, since it sets how strongly each record is fitted: shadows trained differently estimate the wrong IN and OUT distributions. A crude imitation, even shadow data from another distribution, often still works, because “lower loss means member” transfers across tasks (Salem et al. 2019).

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.4 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per record
text:
10.4 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per record
The right comparison is with the same record’s output under models that did and did not train on it. The likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) of Carlini et al. (2022) collects each record’s outputs on IN and OUT shadow models, summarizes each set by a Gaussian, and asks which better explains the target model’s output. The output is \(\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y}\), the log-odds of the confidence \(p_y\) in the true label. Any threshold on confidence, loss or \(\phi\) is the same rule, but for fitting Gaussians \(\phi\) is the right scale: confidences pile up against 1 while their log-odds keep spreading out, and over retrainings \(\phi\) is close to Gaussian.
Let \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}}\) be the mean and standard deviation of \(\phi_z\) over the shadow models that trained on record \(z\), and \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\) over those that did not. Online LiRA scores the observed \(\phi_z\) by the log of how much more likely it is under the IN fit than under the OUT fit, \[\ln\Lambda_z = \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{in}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}}^2\big) - \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{out}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}}^2\big), \tag{10.2}\] where \(\mathcal N(\phi; \mu, \sigma^2)\) is the normal density at \(\phi\), and says “member” above a threshold the same for every record. That is optimal for a simple reason. The attacker sees a record and an output, and the record is drawn the same way whether or not it ends up in training, so it carries no evidence and cancels from the likelihood ratio, leaving the record’s own ratio. Thresholding that is the Neyman–Pearson test, so when the fits are right no attack has a higher TPR at any FPR. Online LiRA needs shadows trained with each target; offline LiRA uses OUT models only, trained once and reused, and scores \((\phi_z - \mu_{\mathrm{out}})/\sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\), how many OUT standard deviations the output lies above its usual value.

One threshold on \(\phi\) must sit high, because typical non-members score high and are 95% of non-members, so atypical members almost never reach it and the TPR is 0.0048. text:
10.5 Evaluating attacks: TPR at a low FPR
Accuracy and the area under the curve (AUC), the probability that a random member outscores a random non-member, average over everyone. A breach is not an average: it is a confident verdict about one person, which requires a low FPR. Attack A recognizes 5% of members with certainty and nobody else; attack B shifts every member’s score slightly. Since the AUC weighs every member–non-member pair equally, a tiny edge on everyone buys as much of it as certainty about a few, and the two have the same AUC (Table 10.2). At FPR \(10^{-3}\) they differ by a factor of 38: A is a severe breach for one person in twenty, B a negligible one for all.

So report the TPR at a low FPR such as \(10^{-3}\), and the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve on log axes, where chance is the diagonal at every scale. Measuring that end takes data: an FPR is a count of false positives, a count of \(k\) has a relative error of about \(1/\sqrt k\), and seeing \(k\) of them at FPR \(\alpha\) takes about \(k/\alpha\) non-members. Give each rate a confidence interval, such as the exact Clopper–Pearson interval. With 5,000 non-members and no false positives you can only bound the FPR by about \(3/5{,}000 = 6\times10^{-4}\).

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.6 Why outliers are most exposed
Only records whose IN and OUT distributions are far apart pass a strict threshold, so they make up the low-FPR end of the curve. Standardize a record’s output against its OUT distribution: if both are Gaussians of common width \(\sigma_z\), a non-member’s output becomes a standard normal and a member’s the same curve shifted by the separation \(s_z\). The best test on that record then has \[\mathrm{TPR}_z(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s_z\big), \qquad s_z = \frac{\mu_{\mathrm{in}} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}}}{\sigma_z}, \tag{10.3}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), so \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\) is the cut-off a non-member exceeds with probability \(\alpha\), about three standard deviations at \(10^{-3}\). A separation of 0.5 leaves a member’s mean far below that cut-off, for a TPR of 0.0048; a separation of 4 puts it beyond, for 0.8185. The numerator is the record’s self-influence, how much training on \(z\) raises the model’s output on \(z\), and it is large when the rest of the data predict the record wrongly.

At FPR \(10^{-3}\), online LiRA flags 26% of outlier members and 0.2% of typical ones (Table 10.4), so 87% of the members it finds are outliers, from 5% of the pool. Outliers whose coin-flip label happens to agree with the trend are predicted correctly unseen and are not exposed (Figure 10.5). So a low loss is normal for an easy record and strong evidence for a hard one.






Figure 10.5: Each pool point’s separation against \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}}\), the mean \(\phi\) of the shadow models that did not train on it. Outliers (triangles) whose label the rest of the data contradict have the largest separations.



The loss attack measures the average self-influence, but the low-FPR end is governed by the largest, so a model with a small gap can still expose a few records completely. Removing the outliers does not fix it. A record’s OUT distribution depends on what the other records predict about it, so exposure is relative: Carlini et al. (2022b) removed the most exposed records, retrained, and found the next layer exposed. A defence has to bound the influence of the worst record, which is what differential privacy does.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.7 Running LiRA on a real model
text:
10.7 Running LiRA on a real model
On an image classifier trained on CIFAR-10, the protocol is the running example’s, with hours of training in place of seconds; Carlini et al. report online LiRA about ten times more powerful than earlier attacks there at low FPR.

Split. For each of \(N + 1\) models choose a random half of the pool. One model plays the target; rotating it gives many (model, record) pairs.
Train every model with the target’s exact recipe, including augmentation.
Statistic. Compute \(\phi\) from the logits, on each record and a few augmented copies.
Fit IN and OUT Gaussians per record over the shadow models.
Score each (target model, record) pair with Equation 10.2, or the offline score.
Evaluate. Pool all pairs, sweep one threshold, plot the ROC curve on log axes, and report the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) with the number of non-member pairs behind it.

With 16 shadow models each record is IN for about 8, too few for per-record variances: on the running example 16 shadows give a TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) of 0.0023 per-record and 0.0151 with a global variance. One target with 25,000 non-member images allows only 25 false positives at that FPR, so rotate over targets. To audit the worst case, plant canaries, records built to be as exposed as possible, as members.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.8 Code
This reproduces the two-kinds example; the last two lines score a typical record’s output 3.244 OUT standard deviations above its OUT mean, exactly on online LiRA’s threshold.
from math import log, pi, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

Z = NormalDist()


def log_normal_pdf(x: float, mu: float, sd: float) -> float:
    return -0.5 * ((x - mu) / sd) ** 2 - log(sd * sqrt(2 * pi))


def lira_online(phi: float, mu_in: float, sd_in: float, mu_out: float, sd_out: float) -> float:
    """Log of how much more likely the target's phi is under the IN fit than under the OUT fit."""
    return log_normal_pdf(phi, mu_in, sd_in) - log_normal_pdf(phi, mu_out, sd_out)


def lira_offline(phi: float, mu_out: float, sd_out: float) -> float:
    """How many OUT standard deviations the target's phi lies above its OUT mean."""
    return (phi - mu_out) / sd_out


def tpr_at_fpr(fpr: float, separation: float) -> float:
    """Best TPR at a given FPR for a record whose IN and OUT scores are unit normals `separation` apart."""
    return 1 - Z.cdf(Z.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - separation)


typical, atypical = tpr_at_fpr(1e-3, 0.5), tpr_at_fpr(1e-3, 4.0)
print(f"{typical:.4f}")  # 0.0048
print(f"{atypical:.4f}")  # 0.8185
print(f"{0.95 * typical + 0.05 * atypical:.4f}")  # 0.0455
print(f"{lira_offline(6.244, 3.0, 1.0):.3f}")  # 3.244
print(f"{lira_online(6.244, 3.5, 1.0, 3.0, 1.0):.3f}")  # 1.497

uv run python code/part02-attacks/membership_inference.py

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model that predicts a lung disease from a patient’s age band and whether they smoke, and puts it behind an interface anyone can query. An insurer knows your age and, from a claim, that you have the disease. Can it use the model to find out whether you smoke? It can guess better than without the model. But that is not yet a privacy failure: if smokers get the disease more often, a published study saying so would allow the same guess about anyone with the disease. The question that matters for you is whether the model reveals more about your attribute because your record was in its training data.
Attribute inference asks an adversary to recover one sensitive field of a record, such as smoking status, a genotype or an income band, from the other fields and access to a model. Model inversion is the classic way to do it: query the model once for each candidate value of the sensitive field, and keep the value that best explains the label you already know.
The one idea: compare with the guesser who never sees the model. Picture a second insurer with no model but perfect knowledge of the population; its best guess from the visible fields is the imputation baseline. A model trained without your record was built from other people’s data only, so it can teach the adversary about the population but nothing about you, and the baseline already assumes the population is known. So for a non-member no attack beats the baseline, while for a member it can. Success up to the baseline is population inference; success on members beyond what non-members get is the leak about individuals. Measuring it means comparing members with non-members, which makes attribute inference a membership question in disguise.
Throughout, a record is \((s, x, y)\): a sensitive attribute \(s\) with a few values, public features \(x\) and a label \(y\). The model’s confidence \(f_y(x, s)\) is the probability it gives label \(y\) at input \((x, s)\).
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.2 The attribute inference game
“The attack recovered 78% of smoking statuses” sounds alarming, but it means nothing until you know how often the attribute could be guessed without the model, and how often the attack succeeds on people who were not in the training set. Yeom et al. (2018) built both comparisons into a game. A challenger trains a model, then flips a fair coin to pick the target either from the training set (a member) or fresh from the population (a non-member). The adversary sees the target’s \(x\) and \(y\) and the model, and guesses \(s\). The score is the difference, \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}} = \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{member}] - \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{non-member}]. \tag{11.1}\] Whatever the attack learned about the population helps members and non-members equally and cancels. What is left is what the model knows about its own training records.
The difference also ties attribute inference to membership. Hand an adversary the whole record and let it say “member” exactly when the attribute attack’s guess is right. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the success on members, its false positive rate (FPR) the success on non-members, and its advantage TPR − FPR is the attribute advantage. So the attribute advantage obeys the membership ceiling, the total variation distance between what the adversary sees for members and for non-members, and a model that leaks nothing about membership leaks nothing about attributes either.
In this chapter’s toy experiment, a logistic regression with a binary sensitive attribute (prior 0.3), ten public features and a binary label is trained on \(n = 100\) records, 200 times. The inversion attack of Section 11.4 is right on 0.7832 of members and 0.7262 of non-members, an advantage of 0.0569 with a standard error of 0.0045. Read as a membership test, its likelihood ratio when it fires is only 1.08 and its balanced accuracy 0.5285. Most of its 78% success would be there if the person had never been in the data. This is also why an attribute attack is a weak membership test at a low FPR: it outputs one bit and is right on most people either way, so a “right” verdict is barely evidence. To measure membership, use the attacks of Membership inference; to report an attribute attack, give its success on members, on non-members and the imputation baseline, never one rate.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.3 The imputation baseline
Population inference is worth measuring directly, since any model of the population, or any published statistic, gives it away. Filling in a missing field from the others is imputation, and the best possible imputation, by a guesser who knows the population exactly, picks for each visible \((x, y)\) the value of \(s\) most probable in the population: the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess. It is the best because, for each visible \((x, y)\), any guess is right exactly on the probability of the value it names, so naming the most probable value wins the most. Many published attribute attacks do no better than imputation from similar data (Jayaraman & Evans 2022).
For a non-member, the model was trained on other people only, so as far as this record goes it is an observation independent of it, and an independent observation cannot change which value of \(s\) is most likely. Every attack therefore satisfies the non-member ceiling \[\Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{non-member}] \le V(S \mid X, Y) = \sum_{x, y}\max_s p(s, x, y), \tag{11.2}\] where \(p(s, x, y)\) is the population probability of a record, and \(V\), the vulnerability, is the success of the MAP guess: for each visible \((x, y)\), the probability of its most likely \(s\), summed. An attack that ignores the model cannot tell the worlds apart at all, because a member, ignoring the model, is just a record drawn from the population. So model-free attacks have zero advantage, and Bayes imputation reaches the ceiling for members and non-members alike.
A worked population makes this concrete. Smoking has prior 0.3; a fraction 0.4 of non-smokers and 0.6 of smokers are old; the disease has probability 0.1, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.7 for young non-smokers, old non-smokers, young smokers and old smokers. The probability of a record is the chance of its smoking status, times the chance of its age band given that, times the chance of its disease outcome given both, which gives Table 11.1.

With no observation the best guess is “non-smoker”, right 0.7 of the time. Age alone changes the probability of smoking but never pushes it past one half, so the guess stays “non-smoker” and the success stays 0.7. Adding the disease pushes the posterior past one half in both disease columns (Figure 11.1), the guess becomes “smoker” there, and the success is the sum of the bold entries, \(V(S \mid X, Y) = 0.748\), a min-entropy leakage of 0.0957 bits. A good model trained on 10,000 patients from this population lets an insurer reach 0.748 on anyone, and no non-member can be attacked better.






Figure 11.1: The posterior probability of smoking in each cell of the smoking table, with each cell’s probability in brackets. Red bars cross \(\frac12\), where imputation guesses “smoker”.



The ceiling is a property of the population, not of the model, and it can be high: if \(x\) and \(y\) nearly determine \(s\), every model and every statistic “reveals” \(s\). That is the “smoking causes cancer” case of Dwork & Roth (2014): the study disclosed a fact about the world, not about its participants. It can still harm people, but no mechanism that limits what one record contributes can prevent it, since the harm would remain with your record removed; it is a question for policy and fairness. In an audit, estimate the baseline with the best imputation model you can fit on data from the same population, and run the attack on held-out non-members too.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.4 Model inversion: the MAP attack
Imputation needs the link \(p(y \mid x, s)\) between label and attribute, and the adversary usually does not know it. But a model that predicts \(y\) from \(x\) and \(s\) is an estimate of exactly that link. Fredrikson et al. (2014) used this on a warfarin dosing model to infer patients’ genetic markers from their demographics and dose, and called it model inversion; confidences make it stronger (Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart 2015). The attack is Bayes’ rule: the value of \(s\) that best explains what you see maximizes “how plausible is \(s\) for someone with these features” times “how likely is the known label if the attribute were \(s\)”. The adversary supplies the first factor from what it knows about the population and gets the second by querying the model at each candidate: \[\hat s(x, y) = \arg\max_s\; p(s \mid x)\, f_y(x, s). \tag{11.3}\] Use \(p(s \mid x)\), not the marginal \(p(s)\) that Fredrikson et al. used, or the attack throws away what \(x\) says about \(s\).
Everything the attack does comes from how the model’s confidences differ from the population’s probabilities. If the model is calibrated, its confidences equal those probabilities, and inversion is imputation, with success \(V(S \mid X, Y)\) on members and non-members alike. Take an old patient with the disease in the smoking table. The adversary knows \(\Pr[\text{smoker} \mid \text{old}] = 0.3913\) and queries a calibrated model, which returns 0.7 for a smoker and 0.3 for a non-smoker. The scores are 0.2739 for “smoker” and 0.1826 for “non-smoker”, so it guesses “smoker”, and normalized they give exactly the posterior 0.6000 of Table 11.1.
A trained model differs from the population in two ways, one per world. On members it is too sure of the truth: training raises the confidence in each record’s label at its true \(s\), while the other value was never paired with that record, so the confidence there stays closer to honest. The ratio that decides the attack is tilted towards the truth, which is overfitting, the generalization gap of Membership inference seen through the sensitive attribute. On non-members the model’s confidences carry the noise of a small training set rather than the population’s exact probabilities, so the attack does worse than imputation. On the toy model, Bayes imputation is right 0.7517 of the time. MAP inversion with the trained model is right on 0.7832 of members, 0.0315 above that ceiling, which no knowledge of the population could produce, and on 0.7262 of non-members, 0.0254 below it. So weak results on fresh records say nothing about members.
More data closes both gaps, because the model approaches the population: the advantage is 0.1610 at \(n = 25\), 0.0111 at \(n = 400\) and 0.0052 at \(n = 1600\) (Figure 11.2).






Figure 11.2: Success of MAP inversion on members and non-members against the training-set size \(n\). Members start above the Bayes imputation ceiling and non-members below it; both converge to the ceiling as the model approaches the population.



The same idea can invert a whole input: on a face recognition model whose classes are people, searching for the image that maximizes one class’s confidence recovers a blurred, recognizable face. That is population inference about the class, and a privacy problem because the class is one person.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.5 Confidence masking
If confidences make inversion stronger, why release them? Rounding them, or returning only the top label, is cheap and leaves the prediction unchanged. Such confidence masking only coarsens what the adversary sees, and whoever sees the full answers could apply the mask themselves, so it can never help the best attacker. For any masking function \(g\) applied to the answers \(F\) the adversary gets by querying every candidate \(s\), \[V\big(S \mid X, Y, g(F)\big) \le V\big(S \mid X, Y, F\big), \tag{11.4}\] on members and on non-members separately. But the inequality says nothing about the difference between the two worlds, which is the leak, and masking lowers each by amounts that need not match.
Labels alone still leak, for the same reason confidences do. On a member, the model usually predicts the training label at the true \(s\), because it fit that record, and an honest label at the other value, so “the label matches at only one candidate” points to the truth. On a non-member the two predicted labels usually agree, and the attack falls back on the guess from \(x\) alone. So masking hurts population inference more than the individual leak. Table 11.2 attacks the same 200 models through three interfaces. Rounding to one decimal changes almost nothing, since the comparison between candidates rarely changes sign. Returning labels only drops non-member success to 0.7092, close to the 0.7045 of guessing from \(x\) alone, while member success stays 0.0224 above the imputation ceiling, so the advantage grows from 0.0569 to 0.0650.

Figure 11.3: MAP inversion success on members and non-members through three interfaces. The dashed line is Bayes imputation, the dotted line the guess from the public features alone.



Masking is obfuscation, not a guarantee: it removes one attack’s input without bounding what any attack learns about a member. So don’t count a drop in overall attack success as a privacy gain; check the member/non-member gap. What shrinks the gap is less overfitting, for example more training data, and what bounds it for every attacker and every output format is differential privacy.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.6 Code
The imputation baseline and the inversion scores of the smoking example take a few lines with the standard library:
from itertools import product
from math import log2

P_SMOKER = 0.3
P_OLD = {0: 0.4, 1: 0.6}  # Pr[old | s]
P_DISEASE = {(0, 0): 0.1, (0, 1): 0.3, (1, 0): 0.4, (1, 1): 0.7}  # Pr[disease | s, old]


def joint(s: int, old: int, disease: int) -> float:
    """Probability of the record (smoker s, old, disease) in the population."""
    p_s = P_SMOKER if s else 1 - P_SMOKER
    p_x = P_OLD[s] if old else 1 - P_OLD[s]
    p_y = P_DISEASE[(s, old)] if disease else 1 - P_DISEASE[(s, old)]
    return p_s * p_x * p_y


def best_guess_success(sees_age: bool, sees_disease: bool) -> float:
    """Success of the MAP guess of s for a guesser who knows the population and sees the chosen fields."""
    cells: dict[tuple[int, int], list[float]] = {}
    for s, old, disease in product((0, 1), repeat=3):
        key = (old if sees_age else -1, disease if sees_disease else -1)
        cells.setdefault(key, [0.0, 0.0])[s] += joint(s, old, disease)
    return sum(max(cell) for cell in cells.values())


def inversion_scores(old: int, confidence: dict[int, float]) -> dict[int, float]:
    """MAP inversion: prior of s given the age band, times the model's confidence in the known label at s."""
    prior = {s: (P_SMOKER if s else 1 - P_SMOKER) * (P_OLD[s] if old else 1 - P_OLD[s]) for s in (0, 1)}
    total = sum(prior.values())
    return {s: prior[s] / total * confidence[s] for s in (0, 1)}


v0, vx, vxy = best_guess_success(False, False), best_guess_success(True, False), best_guess_success(True, True)
print(f"{v0:.4f} {vx:.4f} {vxy:.4f}")  # 0.7000 0.7000 0.7480
print(f"{log2(vxy / v0):.4f}")  # 0.0957
scores = inversion_scores(old=1, confidence={0: 0.3, 1: 0.7})  # a calibrated model, queried for an old patient with the disease
print(f"{scores[1]:.4f} {scores[0]:.4f}")  # 0.2739 0.1826
print(f"{scores[1] / (scores[0] + scores[1]):.4f}")  # 0.6000

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a readmission model on its 1,000 patients and shares it with a research partner. You have checked that no attack can tell, much better than a coin flip, whether any one patient was in the training set. The partner can still learn whether 45% or 55% of the hospital’s patients are over 65, and be right almost every time. That secret is about no patient in particular. It is a property of the training set as a whole, a statistic such as the fraction \(t\) of records in some subgroup, and property inference is the attack that recovers it from a trained model (Ateniese et al. 2015; Ganju et al. 2018).
How can a model hide every record and still give away their mix? Think of it as an average over its \(n\) records, plus noise. The luck of which records were sampled moves an average by about \(1/\sqrt n\); changing one record moves it by about \(1/n\), which is lost in that noise, so membership inference gets harder as \(n\) grows. Changing the subgroup’s share from \(t_0\) to \(t_1\) alters about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records at once, and together they move the model by an amount proportional to \(|t_1 - t_0|\) that does not shrink with \(n\). Against noise of size \(1/\sqrt n\), the signal is about \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\): property inference gets easier with more data. That comparison of scales explains why record-level defences miss properties, why deleting a column does not help, and how to predict an attack’s accuracy before running it.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.2 The property game and its ceiling
text:
12.2 The property game and its ceiling
As for every attack in Threat models and privacy games, write the attack as a game. A challenger flips a fair bit \(b\), draws \(n\) records from a population in which the subgroup has share \(t_b\), trains a model, and hands the attacker the weights (white-box) or answers to queries (black-box). The attacker knows the two shares, has data from both groups, and can train models the way the victim does. It guesses \(b\). Suri & Evans (2022) call this distribution inference.
There is no target record, and that changes the score. A membership attacker faces many targets, and a few exposed with high confidence matter, so you report the true positive rate (TPR) at a low false positive rate (FPR). Here each dataset carries one secret, so the natural score is plain accuracy, the probability of guessing \(b\), against a baseline of \(\frac12\). With a fair bit it equals \(\frac12(1 + \text{advantage})\), where the advantage is \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\).
What is the most any attacker can win? Its only evidence is that some views are more likely under one share than the other, so the best it can do is name the share that makes its view more likely, and that attacker’s advantage is the total variation (TV) distance between the two distributions of the model. The model, being computed from the data, cannot separate the two worlds better than the data do: anyone holding the data could train it and run the same test. When each record shows its group, the only thing in the data that bears on \(t\) is the binomial count of subgroup records. So for every model trained on the data, \[\text{advantage} \le \mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(n, t_0), \mathrm{Bin}(n, t_1)\big). \tag{12.1}\] Releasing the count attains this ceiling, because it keeps everything the data say about \(t\). A model that never sees the group leaks less, and how much less is something you measure.
For the hospital, the count has mean 450 in one world and 550 in the other, with a standard deviation of about 15.7. The means are more than six standard deviations apart, and Equation 12.1 gives 0.9985: an attacker who can read the count off the model is right more than 99.9% of the time. At \(n = 100\) the means are 45 and 55, the standard deviation is about 5, the distributions overlap much more, and the ceiling falls to 0.6827; 200,000 simulated games reach 0.6811.
Whether this is a harm depends on whom the property describes. It arises when the property describes the data owner: one hospital’s patient mix, one company’s customers, one lab’s machines. If the dataset is a small sample of a public population, its property is public anyway.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.3 Why a property leaks when no record does
text:
12.3 Why a property leaks when no record does
On the released count both attackers can be analysed exactly. The membership attacker asks whether its target, a subgroup member, is in the data. The target adds exactly 1 to the count, where the record in its place would add 1 only a fraction \(t\) of the time, so the attacker is looking for one extra unit in a count that already wanders by about \(\sqrt n\). The property attacker asks whether the share was \(t_0\) or \(t_1\); the count’s fraction centres on one or the other, with a spread of about \(\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)/n}\) around the midpoint share \(\bar t = \frac{t_0 + t_1}2\), and what matters is how many spreads separate the centres. With \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, the best advantages are approximately \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{mem}} \approx \frac{1 - t}{\sqrt{2\pi(n - 1)t(1 - t)}}, \qquad \mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{prop}} \approx 2\Phi\Big(\frac{\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|}{2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}}\Big) - 1. \tag{12.2}\] The first is one unit over the spread of the count, so it falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). The second depends on \(n\) and the gap only through \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\), so doubling the gap has the same effect as multiplying \(n\) by 4.
Table 12.1 puts numbers on both; Section 12.6 computes them. At \(n = 10{,}000\) the membership attacker is right with probability \(0.502\), and the property attacker is never wrong to four decimals. The data, the release and the attacker’s knowledge are the same; only the question differs (Figure 12.1).

So a property is a group of records, and a protection measured one record at a time says little about it. For the hospital, moving from 45% to 55% changes 100 of its 1,000 patients, and differential privacy covers groups only through its group-privacy property, whose guarantee weakens with the size of the group (Properties of differential privacy). To hide the property, the release must be noisy on the scale of \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records, and noise that large also destroys what the release was for: hiding the property means hiding the population. Deleting the group column does not escape this, because whatever correlates with the group still changes what the model fits, as the next section shows. And when outsiders contribute training data, audit with poisoning in scope: a few injected records can make the property far easier to infer (Mahloujifar et al. 2022).

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.4 Shadow models and meta-classifiers
For a real model nobody can write down the distribution of the trained weights, so the attacker samples it. It draws many datasets with share \(t_0\) and many with \(t_1\) from auxiliary data, trains a shadow model on each exactly as the victim trains, labels each shadow model’s parameters with its share, and trains a classifier on those parameter vectors, the meta-classifier, which it then applies to the victim’s model. This is the shadow-model recipe of Membership inference, with whole models as the data points.
Which meta-classifier, and how accurate? A model fitted by minimizing an average loss really does behave like an average: its parameters scatter approximately as a Gaussian around the population fit \(\theta(t)\), the model infinitely many records would give, with a covariance \(\Sigma_1/n\) that shrinks like \(1/n\). Between two Gaussians with the same covariance, the quadratic parts of the log-densities cancel and the log-likelihood ratio is linear, so the best test is a hyperplane between the two clouds: train a linear discriminant. Its accuracy depends only on how far apart the centres are in units of the noise. For a small gap they differ by the slope \(\theta'\) of the population fit times the gap, which gives \[\text{accuracy} \approx \Phi\big(\kappa\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|/2\big), \qquad \kappa = \sqrt{\theta'^\top\Sigma_1^{-1}\theta'}. \tag{12.3}\] \(\kappa\) is how fast the model moves with the share, in units of its per-record noise. If the property does not change what the model fits, \(\theta' = 0\) and nothing leaks to first order, however large \(n\) is. If it does, the leak is a side effect of fitting the data well, and no care in the training code removes it. \(\kappa\) also compares any model with the count, whose \(\kappa = 1/\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}\) is 2 at \(\bar t = \frac12\): a model with a smaller \(\kappa\) leaks the property as well as the count would on a fraction \((\kappa\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)})^2\) of its records, the unit in which Suri & Evans (2022) report leakage.
Here is a model that never sees the group and leaks anyway. Records have two features and a label; in the majority risk rises with the second feature, in the subgroup it falls. A logistic regression sees features and labels only. At share \(\frac12\) the two rules cancel in the second weight, and as the subgroup grows its rule wins: the population fit’s second weight moves from 0.442 at share 0.25 to −0.442 at share 0.75. Against that weight’s per-record noise this gives \(\kappa = 0.647\), against 2 for the count, so the model leaks the property as well as \((0.647/2)^2 = 0.105\) of its records would, about one in ten.
With 150 shadow models per hypothesis and 150 fresh target models, the meta-classifier’s accuracy matches Equation 12.3 in most cells of Table 12.2 to within two standard errors, each at most 0.029. Plotted against \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\), the four gaps fall on one curve (Figure 12.2): a gap of 0.05 at \(n = 1{,}000\) is about as easy as a gap of 0.1 at \(n = 200\), since \(\sqrt{1000}\times0.05 = 1.58\) against \(\sqrt{200}\times0.1 = 1.41\).

The misses are where \(n \le 200\) and the gap is at most 0.1. There the true effect is small, the noise in the shadow models swamps it, and the meta-classifier finds the separating direction badly: the attack is weaker than the best test, not the model safer. So an auditor should report the accuracy predicted from \(\kappa\) next to the measured one. Shadow models also need data from both groups, the victim’s algorithm and its dataset size, or they sample the wrong distribution.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.5 Neural networks and permutation invariance
Swap two hidden units of a network, with their incoming and outgoing weights, and it computes the same function. For tanh units, flipping the signs of a unit’s weights in and out also changes nothing, because tanh is odd. Training from a symmetric random start keeps these symmetries, so each weight slot holds a random one of the network’s units with a random sign. The property shows in which units the network has, not in which slot holds which, and averaging slot by slot washes it out: for tanh networks every raw weight has mean zero under both hypotheses, and a linear meta-classifier on raw weights is at chance (Ganju et al. 2018).
The fix is a representation that ignores order and sign. A canonical form flips each unit so its outgoing weight is positive and sorts the units by it; ReLU networks have no sign symmetry, so sorting alone suffices. It is fragile when two units have nearly equal outgoing weights, which swap places from one network to the next. A set representation sums a function of each unit’s parameter vector \(u_j\), and a sum ignores order; \(\sum_ju_ju_j^\top\) ignores signs too, and a learned DeepSets network (Zaheer et al. 2017) is the general form. Probe outputs, the model’s answers on fixed inputs, need no fix: they measure the function, which is what the property changes, and a function does not depend on how it is parameterized. Table 12.3 compares them on tanh networks with 4 hidden units, trained on 200 records with share 0.2 or 0.8, 150 shadow and 150 target networks per side.

The ranking follows the argument, and it means that a meta-classifier at chance on raw weights says the representation is wrong, not that the model is safe, and deeper networks need an invariant representation at every layer. The table also corrects an intuition about access. White-box access is never weaker for the best attack, since whoever holds the weights can compute any query answer, but for a fixed simple attack the representation matters more than the access, and here black-box probes beat raw weights. A model served only through an API is not safe from property inference (Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko 2021).

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.6 Code
The ceiling of Equation 12.1 and the two advantages of Section 12.3 take a few lines:
from math import erf, exp, lgamma, log, sqrt


def binom_pmf(n: int, t: float) -> list[float]:
    """Pr[Bin(n, t) = k] for k = 0..n, in log space so that large n does not overflow."""
    return [exp(lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(k + 1) - lgamma(n - k + 1) + k * log(t) + (n - k) * log(1 - t)) for k in range(n + 1)]


def property_ceiling(n: int, t0: float, t1: float) -> float:
    """Best advantage of any property attack when the group is visible: TV(Bin(n, t0), Bin(n, t1))."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(p - q) for p, q in zip(binom_pmf(n, t0), binom_pmf(n, t1)))


def property_normal(n: int, t0: float, t1: float) -> float:
    """The normal approximation 2 Phi(sqrt(n) |t1 - t0| / (2 sqrt(tbar (1 - tbar)))) - 1."""
    tbar = (t0 + t1) / 2
    z = sqrt(n) * abs(t1 - t0) / (2 * sqrt(tbar * (1 - tbar)))
    return erf(z / sqrt(2))  # equals 2 Phi(z) - 1


def membership_best(n: int, t: float) -> float:
    """Best advantage for one subgroup record from the same count: (1 - t) max_k Pr[Bin(n - 1, t) = k]."""
    return (1 - t) * max(binom_pmf(n - 1, t))


print(f"{property_ceiling(100, 0.45, 0.55):.4f} {property_normal(100, 0.45, 0.55):.4f}")  # 0.6827 0.6827
print(f"{property_ceiling(1000, 0.45, 0.55):.4f} {property_normal(1000, 0.45, 0.55):.4f}")  # 0.9985 0.9984
print(f"{membership_best(100, 0.5):.4f} {membership_best(10000, 0.5):.4f}")  # 0.0398 0.0040

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Why this matters
A language model trained on scraped text sees phone numbers, addresses, keys and private messages. Ask it to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is” and it may finish with the real number. Nothing was breached: the number is stored in the weights and comes out through the normal interface. That is training-data extraction. Membership inference asks whether a record you already hold was in the training set; extraction hands the attacker the record itself, often one it did not know existed.
The idea that organizes the chapter is the rank of a secret under the model. A language model gives every string a probability. Fix the context in which a secret appears, say “my pin is”, and list every possible filler in order of the model’s probability, most likely first. The secret’s rank is its position in that list, and it is also the number of guesses an attacker needs if it tries the most likely fillers first. Memorization is the model putting a training string far above the strings that could have stood in its place. Every measure below reads that rank in its own way.
The examples use one toy: a contact list of 5,000 background lines like toneka 14524 (a made-up name and a five-digit pin), plus 600 secret lines, 100 each repeated 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 times. The model is a character \(n\)-gram model, which predicts each character from the previous \(n - 1\) by counting. Its order \(n\) plays the role of model size.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.2 Verbatim, approximate, discoverable, extractable
“The model memorized its training data” can mean several things, and the numbers differ by orders of magnitude between them, so a report must say which it measures. The definitions differ in what the attacker is assumed to know. A string is extractable (Carlini et al. 2021) if some prompt makes greedy decoding, which appends the most likely next symbol at each step, emit it. That is the real attacker, who has only the model, but measuring it means searching over all prompts. A suffix is discoverable (Carlini et al. 2023) if prompting with its own training prefix makes greedy decoding emit it. That assumes an attacker who holds the prefix, which is strong, but it is easy to measure: prompt with each training prefix and compare. Discoverable implies extractable, since the prefix is one prompt among all. A string is \(k\)-eidetic if it is extractable and appears in at most \(k\) training documents; small \(k\) is the worrying case, a secret seen once and given back.
The definitions also differ in how close the output must be. The ones above are verbatim; a string is approximately memorized (Ippolito et al. 2023) if the output is within some distance of it. Verbatim matching misses near copies, and a phone number with one digit changed has still leaked to anyone who reads it. Ippolito et al. show that prompts which change the style slip approximate copies past a filter that blocks verbatim training text. A verbatim rate is therefore a lower bound on the leak, not a measure of it, and a verbatim filter is not a defence.
Greedy decoding is a convenience for measurement; deployed models sample. A string greedy decoding never emits can still come out. If one sample reproduces it with probability \(p\), then \(m\) independent samples all miss it with probability \((1 - p)^m\), which is at most \(e^{-pm}\), so \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{p} \tag{13.1}\] samples extract it with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). The budget is inversely proportional to \(p\): a string with probability \(10^{-3}\) after its prefix comes out with 99% confidence (\(\beta = 0.01\)) within about 4,600 samples. In the toy, an order-5 model reproduces a secret’s pin in one sample with probability \(1.4\times10^{-3}\) on average at 4 copies and 0.142 at 32 copies, which means 3,252 and 31 samples for a 99% chance. Duplication made the search trivial.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.3 Duplication and model size
Which strings get memorized? In the \(n\)-gram toy the answer can be read off the counts. Greedy decoding follows the largest count at each step, so memorization is a vote. Each copy of a training line adds one vote for the line’s own next symbol in every context the line passes through. The line comes out when, at every step, its votes beat the strongest rival from the rest of the corpus, so the number of copies it needs, \(k^*\), is its largest gap to a rival plus one, set by its most contested step. The fraction of lines memorized at \(k\) copies is the fraction with \(k^* \le k\); this matched greedy decoding exactly in all 36 cells of Table 13.1, because it is a restatement of what greedy decoding does with counts.
Model size works by splitting the vote. A longer context is a finer partition of the training positions: fewer positions share a given context of length 7 than of length 2. So rival counts shrink as the order grows, while the line’s own \(k\) votes stay with it in every context it passes through. In the limit every line has contexts of its own and is memorized from a single copy. That is the toy version of “larger models memorize more”: a larger model can afford to give rare strings parameters of their own.
Table 13.1 shows both effects. Along a row, at order 5, the verbatim rate climbs from 0 at one copy to 0.70 at 32. Down a column, a line seen once is safe up to order 5, memorized 8% of the time at order 6, 70% at order 7 and 98% at order 8; those singletons are 1-eidetic.

For real models, Carlini et al. (2023) found that discoverable memorization grows log-linearly with duplication, model size and prompt length, and that the largest model they measured, GPT-J, reproduces at least 1% of its training data from 50-token prefixes.
The vote picture also says who is exposed first. A line whose name shares little with other names reaches a context of its own sooner, so rare and atypical strings are memorized first; this is the high self-influence of atypical examples from Algorithmic stability and generalization, which can only be fitted by memorizing them. Deduplication lowers \(k\) for every repeated string, so it is the cheapest defence: Lee et al. (2022) found that models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often without losing quality. But it cannot touch a singleton in a large model, where \(k = 1\) already suffices; deduplicating the order-8 model’s data would barely change its 98%. And because larger models memorize from fewer copies, an audit passed at one size must be redone after scaling up.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.4 Canaries and the exposure metric
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing; an auditor wants a graded answer with a known false alarm rate. Carlini et al. (2019) plant canaries, random secrets of a fixed format such as “my pin is” followed by five random digits, in the training data, then read off the trained model’s rank of the canary among all values of that format. Because you chose the canary at random, you know the answer and the size of the space \(\mathcal R\). The exposure reads the rank on a log scale, \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.2}\] Before seeing the model, an attacker guessing the canary faces \(|\mathcal R|\) equally likely values; guessing in the model’s order, it needs \(\operatorname{rank}\) tries. Exposure is the difference in bits, the number of halvings of the search the model has done for the attacker.
What makes exposure an audit tool is that its behaviour without memorization is known exactly. If the model does not depend on the canary, for instance because it was never inserted, the canary is just a uniformly random value, so its rank is uniform over the list. The chance of landing in the top fraction \(2^{-e}\) of the list is then \(2^{-e}\): \[\Pr[\mathrm{exposure} \ge e] \le 2^{-e}. \tag{13.3}\] So exposure is \(-\log_2\) of a p-value, and the test “inserted if exposure \(\ge e\)” has false positive rate (FPR) at most \(2^{-e}\). “Was this canary inserted?” is a membership question, but where membership inference calibrates its test with shadow models, here the canary’s own randomness does the calibration. In the toy, uninserted pins show mean exposure 1.443 bits, the \(\log_2 e\) the uniform rank predicts, and a fraction \(1/32 = 2^{-5}\) with exposure at least 5.
For “my pin is 58745”, \(|\mathcal R| = 10^5\) and the maximum exposure is 16.61 bits. Table 13.2 gives the exact exposure, from scoring all \(10^5\) pins. The order-4 model reaches the maximum at 16 copies. The order-2 model barely moves even at 64, because its one-character contexts are shared with every line, the vote-splitting argument run backwards.

For a large space the rank must be estimated. Counting how many of \(m\) random candidates score above the canary is reliable, but a canary above all of them only says its rank fraction is below about \(1/m\), so it cannot resolve exposures above \(\log_2 m\). Fitting a distribution to the scores reaches further, but only as far as its tail is right, and the tail is the part you cannot sample. At order 3 with 8 copies, counting 10,000 random pins gives 5.35 bits against an exact 5.24, while a normal fit gives 8.28, because the scores have a heavier right tail than a normal. Ties are a further trap: a model that has never seen a context gives every candidate the same score, so every rank is the last and every exposure 0, which hides rather than measures.
Because you control what was planted, use canaries to compare training runs that differ in one thing: with and without deduplication, before and after an unlearning method, or with private training (Part 3). Carlini et al. (2019) found that differentially private training kept their canaries at the exposure of canaries never inserted.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
A real attacker has only the model. Carlini et al. (2021) extracted training data from GPT-2 in three steps: generate many samples, rank them by how likely they are to be memorized, and verify the top of the ranking against a search or public sources. The ranking is the hard step, and it is a hypothesis test. A model can find a string likely because text like it is common, or because it memorized it, and only the second is a leak. Ranking by the target’s likelihood alone surfaces the common, such as licences and boilerplate, which reveal nothing. A reference model, trained on similar data that excludes the target’s training set, stands in for “common text”, and the right score is how much more likely the target finds \(x\) than the reference does: \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x). \tag{13.4}\] Text both models know cancels. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing, this likelihood ratio is the most powerful ranking at every FPR; it is the per-example calibration of membership inference again. The reference can be crude: a smaller model of the same family, the zlib-compressed length of the text, or the target’s own likelihood on the lowercased text.
In the toy, the attacker draws 20,000 lines from the order-6 model, whose training set also contains 50 public lines repeated 100 times each. Among the 14,852 distinct samples are 197 private training lines. Of the top 100 by likelihood only 45 are private, since the public lines are the most likely strings the model knows. Ranked by Equation 13.4, with a reference trained on an independent contact list that also contains the public lines, 85 of the top 100 are private (Figure 13.2).






Figure 13.2: Fraction of the top-ranked distinct generations that are private training lines (solid) or public lines (dashed), from 20,000 samples of an order-6 model. Ranking by likelihood puts the public lines first; ranking by the likelihood ratio to a reference model puts the private lines first.



Without the prefix the attacker gets much less than is discoverable: none of the secrets inserted 1, 2 or 4 times appear in the samples, though 76% of the 4-copy secrets are discoverable at order 6. A sample must first produce the right name before it can produce the pin, and only heavily duplicated lines make their names likely enough.
“Less than discoverable” can still be a great deal. Nasr et al. (2023) attacked an aligned chat model, which rarely emits training data in normal use because alignment taught it to answer as an assistant, not to continue documents. Asked to repeat a single word forever, it diverged into text that looked like pretraining documents; about 200 US dollars of queries extracted over 10,000 unique memorized examples, including personal contact details. Alignment changed how the model usually responds, not what it had memorized, so it is not a defence, and a red team should test prompts that escape the chat behaviour. Verify outputs against the training set, or against a large public corpus as a lower bound. Report precision at the top of the ranking, which is the low-FPR operating point an attacker checking candidates by hand cares about, not recall over all memorized strings.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 Why this matters
A phone keyboard learns from what its users type, and the raw text never leaves the phones. The server sends the current model to each phone, the phone computes the gradient of the loss on its own few examples, and only that gradient goes back. This is federated learning (FL), often described as private because “the data stay on the device”. If you design, review or red-team such a system, the question is: what does one client’s gradient reveal about the client’s data?
Often, everything, because many entries of a gradient are simple functions of the input. Take a fully connected layer, which computes \(a = Wx + b\). The weight \(W_{jk}\) multiplies the input \(x_k\), so nudging \(W_{jk}\) changes \(a_j\) by \(x_k\) times the nudge, and the loss responds to \(a_j\) at some rate \(\delta_j = \partial\ell/\partial a_j\) set by everything above the layer. The chain rule multiplies the two rates, and the bias, which is added to \(a_j\) directly, gets \(\delta_j\) alone: \[\nabla_W\ell = \delta\,x^\top, \qquad \nabla_b\ell = \delta. \tag{14.1}\] The weight gradient is an outer product: row \(j\) is the input \(x\) scaled by the single number \(\delta_j\), so the layer’s input sits in every row. The rest of the network, the loss and the label only set the scales. With one example the scale can be divided out; with a batch the gradient is a sum of one outer product per example, and the attacker’s job is to pull the sum apart.
The attacker here is an honest-but-curious server in the sense of Threat models and privacy games: it follows the protocol, sends the real model and only analyses what it receives. It knows the architecture and every parameter, because it chose them, and it sees each client’s update \(g = \frac1B\sum_i\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i)\), the average gradient over the client’s \(B\) examples. Reconstructions are scored by the relative error \(\lVert\hat x - x\rVert/\lVert x\rVert\) against the closest true example. The experiments use \(8\times8\) images of four shapes and a network with one hidden layer of 32 units at its random initialization: 2,212 gradient entries against 64 unknown pixels per example.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.2 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.2 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
For a single example, Equation 14.1 already gives the attack (Phong et al. 2018). Row \(j\) of the first layer’s weight gradient is \(\delta_{1,j}x^\top\), and entry \(j\) of its bias gradient is the same number \(\delta_{1,j}\), so dividing one by the other cancels the only unknown scale. Every unit \(j\) with a nonzero bias gradient gives \[x = \frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. \tag{14.2}\] No search, no prior on the data and no label are needed, and the attack checks itself: all usable units must give the same answer, so if their ratios agree, the attacker knows it has the input.
Take a two-unit ReLU network with \(W_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.4 & -0.2 & 0.1\\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.4\end{pmatrix}\), \(b_1 = (0.1, -0.1)\), \(W_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}\) and no output bias, and an input \(x = (0.5, 1, 0.2)\) with the first class as label. The backward signal at the first layer is \(\delta_1 = (-0.3279, 0.9838)\), so the two rows of the weight gradient are \((-0.1640, -0.3279, -0.0656)\) and \((0.4919, 0.9838, 0.1968)\), visibly the same vector at two scales. Dividing each by its bias entry gives \((0.5, 1, 0.2)\) twice; Section 14.6 runs it. On an \(8\times8\) image and the 32-unit network, 13 units are switched on, and each of the 13 ratios equals the image to a relative error of at most \(6.7\times10^{-17}\), rounding error (Figure 14.1).






Figure 14.1: Exact recovery from the first-layer gradient of a ReLU network with 32 hidden units. Left: the client’s input. Middle: the weight gradient, one row per hidden unit, next to the bias gradient; every nonzero row is the image times its bias entry, and switched-off units give zero rows. Right: one row divided by its bias entry, which is the input exactly.



Because the division cancels \(\delta_1\), whatever produced \(\delta_1\) is irrelevant: twenty layers above the first, or a custom loss, change nothing. A ReLU unit switched off on \(x\) has \(\delta_{1,j} = 0\) and gives nothing, but one active unit is enough. Without a bias there is no denominator, yet every row still points along \(x\), so \(x\) is known up to one number that a one-dimensional search finds. The same division at a deeper fully connected layer yields that layer’s input, an intermediate feature vector. What really breaks the closed form is a convolutional first layer: a convolution applies one small filter at every position of the image, so its gradient is a sum of outer products over all the image patches, and no single division separates them. A batch of more than one example is a sum too, and breaks it only partly (Section 14.5).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.3 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.3 Label recovery from the last layer
The label is often the most sensitive part of an example (the diagnosis, the next word typed), and the last layer gives it away by a sign (Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen 2020). With softmax and cross-entropy, the backward signal at the logits is the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot label, \(p - e_y\). Softmax probabilities lie strictly between 0 and 1, so every entry is positive except the one at the true label, \(p_y - 1\). By Equation 14.1 the last-layer bias gradient is exactly this signal, so for one example the label is the position of its only negative entry: \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.3}\] Without a bias the weight gradient tells the same story: its row \(k\) is the signal’s entry \(k\) times the hidden activations, and if those are never negative (ReLU or sigmoid) the multiplication keeps the sign, so the label is the only row with a negative sum. Both rules were right in 1,000 of 1,000 trials. Nothing in the argument depends on how good the model is, so they are exact at any point of training; only a probability that rounds to 1 in floating point hides the sign.
For a batch of \(B\), the bias gradient is the average of \(p_i - e_{y_i}\). The one-hot parts add up to the label histogram, and the probability parts to the model’s total predicted probability for each class, so the number \(n_k\) of examples of class \(k\) is \[n_k = \sum_{i=1}^Bp_{ik} - B\,(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.4}\] The equation is exact; the only unknown is the total prediction \(\sum_ip_{ik}\). The attacker knows the model, so it estimates that total as \(B\) times the model’s average prediction on data of its own, and rounds. Since true counts are integers, rounding is exact whenever the estimate is off by less than one half for every class.
A batch of 16 has true counts \((4, 2, 4, 6)\). With the average prediction taken over 200 of the attacker’s own images, Equation 14.4 gives \((3.88, 2.00, 4.19, 5.92)\), which rounds to the truth. Assuming the model predicts every class equally gives \((2.12, 3.01, 4.27, 6.60)\), which does not, because even an untrained network is not uniform. Over 200 random batches, the averaged estimate gets all counts exact for 1.000 of batches of 4, 0.975 of batches of 16 and 0.525 of batches of 64 (Figure 14.2): the error of the estimate grows with \(B\), and once it passes one half, rounding starts to miss, though the counts stay close.






Figure 14.2: Labels from the last-layer bias gradient. Left: for one example it has a single negative entry, at the true label. Right: for a batch of 16, the counts estimated with the model’s average prediction on the attacker’s own images are close to the true counts; with a uniform guess they are off by up to about half an example.



So a batch leaks its label histogram even when no input is recovered. And knowing the label helps the next attack: it removes a discrete unknown, so the search of Section 14.4 runs over the input only.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.4 Deep Leakage from Gradients
Convolutions, normalization layers or missing biases leave no closed form. Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG) (Zhu, Liu & Han 2019) needs none: guess an input, compute the gradient it would produce, and move the guess until that gradient matches the one observed. If only the true input produces the observed gradient, a matching guess is the input. With the labels fixed as above, DLG minimizes the matching loss, the squared distance between the gradient of the guessed batch and \(g\): \[\hat x = \arg\min_{x'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\lVert\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\rVert^2. \tag{14.5}\] It starts from random noise and runs a gradient method on \(R\), which automatic differentiation provides by differentiating through the backward pass.
Two consequences follow from that construction. Since \(R\) is built from gradients, its own gradient is made of second derivatives of the network. ReLU’s slope is constant on each side of zero, so its second derivative is zero almost everywhere and the search gets no signal through it; that is why Zhu et al. replaced ReLU by the sigmoid, as the experiments here do. And since the true input has \(R = 0\), the smallest possible value, the final \(R\) reports the outcome: at rounding error the match is exact, while a loss that stopped falling well above zero means the search is stuck, because \(R\) is not convex.
On one image, the sigmoid network with 32 hidden units, and 600 steps of the Adam optimizer from uniform noise, the relative error is \(7.5\times10^{-2}\) at step 50, already visually correct, and \(5.8\times10^{-14}\) at step 600, with matching loss \(1.3\times10^{-27}\) (Figure 14.3).






Figure 14.3: Deep Leakage from Gradients on one image, sigmoid network with 32 hidden units. Top: the reconstruction at selected iterations, starting from noise, and the true input. Bottom: the matching loss and the relative error on a log scale; both fall until they reach rounding error.



A failed run is therefore an optimization failure, not evidence of privacy, and the attacker sees it and retries with restarts, better optimizers or image priors. Geiping et al. (2020), comparing gradients by cosine distance and penalizing differences between neighbouring pixels, recover recognizable images from trained networks and from batches.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.5 Batches and averaging
Clients usually send a batch average, and averaging is often said to protect individuals: the gradient describes the batch, not anyone in it. Averaging does break Equation 14.2 and makes DLG harder, but the outer-product structure survives it.
The first-layer gradient is now a sum of \(B\) outer products, one per example. Every row is a combination of the \(B\) inputs, and the matrix has rank at most \(B\), so the server learns the subspace that contains the batch, which for \(B\) much smaller than the input dimension already rules out almost every input. A unit’s ratio from Equation 14.2 is now a weighted average of the inputs, each weighted by its share of the unit’s backward signal, and it equals one input exactly when the unit is active for that example only, when it isolates it. If each of \(m\) ReLU units fires on each example like an independent fair coin, a unit isolates a given example with probability \(2^{-B}\), and the example escapes only if all \(m\) units miss it: \[P_{\text{iso}}(B, m) = 1 - (1 - 2^{-B})^m. \tag{14.6}\] Each extra example halves the chance per unit, and each extra unit adds a chance. An even chance at \(B = 10\) needs 710 units, and real first layers have thousands.
A batch of 4 through the 32-unit ReLU network gives a rank-4 gradient, and the unit ratios recover all 4 images exactly, where the formula predicts 0.873 per example. Table 14.1 tests the formula more widely. For Gaussian inputs, whose units really do fire like coins, it matches. For images it is far too optimistic about privacy at large batches: at \(B = 16\) in the 1024-unit network it predicts 1.6% exposed, and 69.1% is. Images are correlated, so a unit tends to fire on many of them or on few, and units that fire on exactly one are much more common than coin flips allow (Figure 14.4).

DLG has to untangle \(B\) inputs from one sum. On the sigmoid network it recovers all single images, 0.67 of examples in batches of 2, 0.29 at \(B = 4\) and none at \(B = 8\), where the matching loss stalls near \(10^{-5}\) and the reconstructions are blends. That is a stuck search, not missing information: 2,212 equations remain.
So batching is not a defence. The label histogram, the span and every isolated example come out exactly. Sending the parameter change after several local steps does not help either: every step’s first-layer gradient is built from outer products with the same inputs, so for one example the change is still a multiple of \(x^\top\) in every row, and the division still recovers \(x\). And all of this is what an honest server can do with random weights. A malicious server chooses the weights, and can plant units that fire on rare inputs only (Boenisch et al. 2023) or that sort inputs into bins by a feature (Fowl et al. 2022), so that most of a large batch is isolated by design. Defences have to change what the server sees: differential privacy (Part 3) bounds what any update reveals, and secure aggregation, which reveals only the sum over many clients, is introduced in Local, shuffle and distributed trust models.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Code
The hand example of Section 14.2, with the label rule and the isolation formula, in plain Python. The script indexes classes from 0, so label 0 is the first class.
from math import ceil, exp, log

Vector = list[float]
Matrix = list[Vector]


def client_gradient(w1: Matrix, b1: Vector, w2: Matrix, x: Vector, y: int) -> tuple[Matrix, Vector, Vector]:
    """What a client sends for one example: the gradients of W1, b1 and b2 (one ReLU layer, softmax, cross-entropy)."""
    a = [sum(wk * xk for wk, xk in zip(row, x)) + bj for row, bj in zip(w1, b1)]
    h = [max(aj, 0.0) for aj in a]
    z = [sum(wk * hk for wk, hk in zip(row, h)) for row in w2]
    total = sum(exp(zk) for zk in z)
    delta2 = [exp(zk) / total - (1.0 if k == y else 0.0) for k, zk in enumerate(z)]  # p - e_y
    delta1 = [sum(delta2[k] * w2[k][j] for k in range(len(w2))) * (1.0 if a[j] > 0 else 0.0) for j in range(len(a))]
    grad_w1 = [[dj * xk for xk in x] for dj in delta1]  # outer product delta1 x^T
    return grad_w1, delta1, delta2  # the bias gradients equal the backward signals


def recover_input(grad_w1: Matrix, grad_b1: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Exact recovery: a row of the weight gradient divided by its bias entry."""
    j = next(j for j, g in enumerate(grad_b1) if g != 0.0)
    return [g / grad_b1[j] for g in grad_w1[j]]


def recover_label(grad_b2: Vector) -> int:
    """The only negative entry of the last-layer bias gradient is the label."""
    return min(range(len(grad_b2)), key=lambda k: grad_b2[k])


def isolation(batch: int, units: int) -> float:
    """Chance that some ReLU unit fires for one given example of the batch only, under the coin-flip model."""
    return 1 - (1 - 2.0**-batch) ** units


def width_for_even_odds(batch: int) -> int:
    """Smallest number of units that isolates each example with probability at least 1/2."""
    return ceil(log(2) / -log(1 - 2.0**-batch))


w1 = [[0.4, -0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.5, -0.4]]
b1 = [0.1, -0.1]
w2 = [[1.0, -1.0], [0.5, 0.5]]
gw1, gb1, gb2 = client_gradient(w1, b1, w2, x=[0.5, 1.0, 0.2], y=0)
print([round(v, 4) for v in recover_input(gw1, gb1)])  # [0.5, 1.0, 0.2]
print([round(v, 4) for v in gb2], recover_label(gb2))  # [-0.6559, 0.6559] 0
print(f"{isolation(4, 32):.3f}")  # 0.873
print(width_for_even_odds(10))  # 710

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Why this matters
A hospital shares its discharge records with researchers after deleting names and addresses, keeping postcode, date of birth, sex and diagnosis. But most people are the only person with their postcode, birth date and sex, so anyone holding a table with names and those three columns, such as a voter roll, can join the two and put a name back on most rows. This is a linkage attack, and naming a “de-identified” record is re-identification. It needs only the release and some auxiliary data, so run it before you sign off on sharing a dataset.
What makes it work is that identifying information is measured in bits, and bits add up. Picking one person out of \(n\) takes \(\log_2 n\) bits, because each bit halves the candidates: 27.9 bits for the 248.7 million people in the United States in 1990, 32.9 for 8 billion. An attribute with \(v\) equally likely values carries at most \(\log_2 v\) bits, and for independent attributes the bits add, because probabilities multiply and the logarithm turns the product into a sum. Once the bits an adversary knows exceed \(\log_2 n\) by a few, almost everyone is unique.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.2 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
Direct identifiers, such as a name, name a person on their own. Sensitive attributes, such as a diagnosis, are what the release is about. Quasi-identifiers sit in between: they name nobody alone, but in combination they single people out, and they also appear in other datasets next to names. ZIP code, birth date and sex are the classic example. Deleting the first kind and keeping the third is the most common form of “de-identification”, and linkage is aimed at exactly that gap.
Group the records of a release into equivalence classes, sets of records with identical quasi-identifiers. An adversary who knows the target is in the release, and knows the target’s quasi-identifiers, finds the target’s class and picks a record from it: right for sure if the class has one record, one time in \(k\) if it has \(k\). Each class therefore contributes exactly one record’s worth of wins however large it is, and the best possible success is \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n}, \tag{15.1}\] the number \(J\) of distinct quasi-identifier combinations divided by the number \(n\) of records.

Join Table 15.1 with Table 15.2. Ana, Carla and Dan are each alone in their class, so their diagnoses come out with certainty; Ben shares his class with one other record, so the adversary is right about him half the time. The classes have sizes 1, 1, 1, 2 and 3, so \(J = 5\) for \(n = 8\) and the success is \(5/8 = 0.625\). Sweeney re-identified the governor of Massachusetts this way in the late 1990s: on the Cambridge voter roll, six people shared his birth date, three were men, and one lived in his ZIP code.
Every unique record is a certain win, so the fraction of unique records is a floor on the success, and predicting uniqueness is the core of a risk assessment. Conversely, if every class has at least \(k\) records then \(J \le n/k\) and the success is at most \(1/k\). That is the promise of k-anonymity, and it holds against this adversary only: had all three women born on 1990-01-01 had asthma, the adversary would learn it without picking a record, the gap studied in Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks. And which columns are quasi-identifiers is not a property of the table but a guess about what auxiliary data exist; in sparse data, every column is one (Section 15.4).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.3 How many people are unique?
To predict uniqueness for a release not yet made, use a model of the population. Call a person’s combination of attribute values their cell, and suppose each person falls in cell \(c\) with probability \(p_c\), independently. A person in cell \(c\) is unique when all \(n - 1\) others land elsewhere, which happens with probability \((1 - p_c)^{n-1}\); averaging over the person’s own cell gives the expected fraction unique, \[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} = \sum_c p_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}. \tag{15.2}\]
With \(M\) equally likely cells this becomes the bits picture. Each person stays alone with probability about \(e^{-n/M}\), where \(n/M\) is the average occupancy of a cell. With \(b = \log_2 M\) bits the occupancy is \(2^{\log_2 n - b}\), so the fraction unique is about \(\exp(-2^{\log_2 n - b})\): it depends only on the bits beyond the \(\log_2 n\) needed to name one person, the same curve for a town and for the planet (Figure 15.1, right). Every extra bit halves the occupancy, so the curve is steep: half the people are unique at 0.53 bits beyond \(\log_2 n\), 99% at 6.64 bits beyond.
So “33 bits identify anyone” is misleading: 33 bits for 8 billion people put about one person in the average cell, where only a fraction 0.394 is unique, because random labels collide often. 99% uniqueness takes 39.5 bits.
Sweeney’s attributes show the accounting. About 40,000 ZIP codes are worth 15.3 bits, a birth date over 80 years 14.8, and sex 1.0: at most 31.1 bits against the 27.9 that single out one American, so about 0.106 people per cell and a uniqueness of \(e^{-0.106} = 0.899\) if cells were equally likely. From 1990 census tables she estimated 87%. The gap is skew: people crowd into popular cells, which hold nobody unique, while rare cells stay empty. Correlation pulls the same way, because correlated attributes (ZIP code and income) say partly the same thing, so their joint bits are less than the sum. A bits sum is a quick screen, not an estimate. Table 15.3 reveals the attributes of a synthetic census of 10,000 people one at a time (\(\log_2 n = 13.29\) bits).
